chapters.title: Flexbox: one-dimensional layout and resilient navigation
key_terms: Flex container
An element with `display: flex` whose direct children become flex items laid out along one axis.
Main axis
The direction in which a flex container places its items, set by `flex-direction`.
Cross axis
The axis perpendicular to the main axis, along which `align-items` positions the items.
Flex basis
An item's starting size along the main axis before free space is distributed or taken away.
Flex wrap
The `flex-wrap: wrap` setting that moves items onto new lines instead of shrinking or overflowing.
chapters.mental:
Flexbox distributes space among items primarily along one axis. The main axis follows flex-direction, while the cross axis is perpendicular. justify-content distributes available space along the main axis; align-items aligns items along the cross axis. The names do not permanently mean horizontal and vertical because direction can change.

Flexible items have a basis and rules for growing or shrinking. A row of long labels may overflow if wrapping is disabled or if an item's automatic minimum size prevents shrinking. `min-inline-size:0` is often useful for a flex child that must allow its text to wrap or truncate deliberately. Flexbox is a layout tool, not permission to reorder content into a confusing keyboard sequence.
chapters.anatomy: Use display:flex, gap and flex-wrap:wrap for a simple responsive group. `flex: 1 1 12rem` gives an initial basis and permits growth and shrinkage. Set `align-items:stretch` when equal cross-axis size supports the component. Keep DOM order aligned with intended reading and focus order rather than using order to create a contradictory visual sequence.
examples: Wrapping preserves reachable links when space is limited.
Items form additional rows rather than overflowing.
The basis expresses a preference rather than an inflexible width.
Cards share available space and can wrap.
tasks: Name the axes for flex-direction:column.
The main axis is vertical in the usual horizontal writing mode; the cross axis is horizontal.
The main axis follows flex-direction; the cross axis is perpendicular to it.
flex-direction: column makes the main axis vertical, so justify-content distributes items vertically and align-items aligns them horizontally.
Add gap between navigation items without per-item margins.
Spacing is owned by the container and stays consistent when wrapping.
Replace the per-item margins with one gap declaration on the container.
gap adds space only between items, including after wrapping, so the outer edges stay flush.
Build a wrapping navigation bar and flexible card row.
Long labels stay reachable at narrow widths and DOM order remains logical.
Use flex-wrap: wrap and let each item size itself from its content.
Wrapping moves items to a new line instead of overflowing, while source order keeps reading and focus order logical.
Diagnose a flex child that refuses to shrink.
Inspect its minimum size, long content and flex-basis before forcing overflow hidden.
Check the item's automatic minimum width and any long unbreakable word.
Flex items default to min-width: auto, so they will not shrink below their longest content until you set min-width: 0 or allow wrapping.
Test one item, many items and a very long label.
The layout remains readable without relying on exactly three equal strings.
Change the number of items and the length of the longest label before calling the layout done.
A layout tuned for three equal labels can overflow or wrap badly when the content changes.
Explain when Flexbox fits better than Grid.
Use Flexbox for distributing items along one primary dimension; use Grid for explicit two-dimensional alignment.
Ask whether you are aligning items along one line or in rows and columns at the same time.
Flexbox distributes items along one axis based on their content, while Grid places items in explicit rows and columns.
chapters.mistakes: Do not equate justify-content with horizontal alignment universally. Visual order changes do not necessarily change keyboard order. A perfectly aligned screenshot is insufficient if navigation becomes confusing.

reasoning.approach: Note that `flex-direction: column` sets the main axis along the block direction, so in horizontal writing it runs top to bottom.
reasoning.pitfall: Assuming `justify-content` still aligns horizontally fails because it always follows the main axis, which is now vertical.
reasoning.verify: With a fixed container height, `justify-content: center` moves items vertically and `align-items: center` moves them horizontally.

reasoning.approach: Remove per-item margins and set `gap: 0.75rem` on the flex container so spacing applies only between items.
reasoning.pitfall: Keeping `margin-right` on every link fails because the last item gets extra trailing space and wrapped rows start misaligned.
reasoning.verify: When the links wrap, the first link on each row lines up with the container edge and gaps look equal.

reasoning.approach: Use a wrapping flex `ul` for navigation and a wrapping flex container for cards with `flex: 1 1 12rem` and `min-inline-size: 0`.
reasoning.pitfall: Using the `order` property to move the last link first fails because keyboard focus still follows DOM order and seems to jump.
reasoning.verify: At the narrow preset every link is visible, and pressing Tab visits them in the same order they appear.

reasoning.approach: Inspect the child's computed `min-width`, its longest word and its `flex-basis` before changing anything.
reasoning.pitfall: Adding `overflow: hidden` to the parent fails because it hides the overflow and the clipped text silently becomes unreadable.
reasoning.verify: After setting `min-inline-size: 0`, the item's computed width is below its content width and nothing is clipped.

reasoning.approach: Run three fixtures: a single item, twelve items and one item with a very long label, at both wide and narrow widths.
reasoning.pitfall: Testing with three equal labels fails because it never exercises wrapping or the content-based minimum that real labels trigger.
reasoning.verify: Each fixture shows no horizontal page scrollbar and every label is fully readable.

reasoning.approach: Ask whether items only need to line up along one row or column, or whether rows and columns must align with each other.
reasoning.pitfall: Using Flexbox for a card grid with aligned columns fails because each wrapped row sizes independently, so columns drift.
reasoning.verify: In a wrapped flex row of unequal cards, edges in different rows do not line up, while Grid aligns them.

contrast.heading: a flex item that refuses to shrink
contrast.setup: A card contains one long unbroken identifier. Compare the card before and after setting a minimum size.
contrast.reading: Flex items default to `min-width: auto`, which in practice means they cannot shrink below their longest unbreakable content. A 60-character identifier therefore forces its card wider than the shared space, and the row overflows the container even though `flex-shrink` is 1. Setting `min-inline-size: 0` removes that floor, and `overflow-wrap: anywhere` lets the identifier break so the card can actually use the narrower width. Remove only the first repair line and you will see the card still overflow, because the wrap rule alone cannot beat the automatic minimum.

chapters.title: Grid: tracks, gaps and two-dimensional alignment
key_terms: Grid container
An element with `display: grid` that places its children into rows and columns.
Track
One row or column of a grid, sized by `grid-template-columns` or `grid-template-rows`.
Fr unit
A flexible length that shares a grid container's free space among tracks in proportion to their fr values.
Minmax
The `minmax()` function that gives a track a minimum and a maximum size, such as `minmax(12rem, 1fr)`.
Auto-fit
The `repeat()` keyword that creates as many tracks as fit and collapses empty ones so the filled tracks stretch.
chapters.mental:
Grid arranges items along rows and columns. A track is the space between two adjacent grid lines. Fractional fr units share remaining space after fixed sizes and gaps have been considered. They are not a fixed percentage of the full container. An item's minimum content contribution can still affect track size, which explains why a long unbroken value may widen an apparently equal grid.

Grid is useful when rows and columns must align across a collection. An auto-fit repeat with minmax can create as many columns as fit a preferred minimum, then distribute remaining room. The minimum must still fit a narrow viewport. A layout should adapt to its content, not depend on one device model or a fixed card count.
chapters.anatomy: Use `grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fit,minmax(min(100%,14rem),1fr))` for a resilient card collection. The inner min permits a track to fit a container narrower than the preferred minimum. `gap` adds separation without changing source order. Named grid areas are useful for a page shell, but the source order must remain understandable when the layout collapses.

Two tracks share the available width without an automatic min-content floor.
The preferred minimum is bounded by the available width.
The column count adapts to available space.
tasks: Explain why two 1fr tracks plus a gap are not two 50% widths plus a gap.
Fractional tracks divide the remaining space after the gap.
Subtract the gap from the container width before dividing anything.

Add a fourth card without new positional rules.
Auto placement incorporates the item using the same layout contract.
Add the card to the markup and leave the grid rule unchanged.
Auto placement fills the next available cell, so the existing column definition decides where a new item goes.
Build an adaptive topic grid that survives a narrow container.
Cards change column count while preserving reading order and avoiding page overflow.
Use repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 14rem), 1fr)) and resize the preview.
minmax with min(100%, 14rem) lets each track shrink to the container width on narrow screens, and auto-fit chooses the column count from the available space.
Diagnose a long value widening a track.
Inspect minimum content sizing and use a deliberate minmax or wrapping policy.
Check whether the track uses auto or 1fr, whose minimum is the longest content.
A 1fr track has an automatic minimum equal to its min-content size, so minmax(0, 1fr) or wrapping is needed to stop one long value from widening it.
Test empty, one-card and seven-card collections.
The layout remains coherent without a special case tied to three cards.
Render zero, one and seven cards with the same CSS.
Intrinsic grid rules adapt to any item count, while rules written for exactly three cards break when content changes.
Explain auto-fit versus auto-fill at a high level.
Auto-fit can collapse empty repeated tracks; auto-fill preserves the generated track slots.
Make the container much wider than all cards need and compare the two keywords.
auto-fill keeps empty tracks reserved, while auto-fit collapses empty tracks so the existing cards stretch to fill the row.
chapters.mistakes: Do not use visual grid placement to conceal an incoherent document order. Avoid a minimum track width larger than the smallest intended container. Fr units are space-sharing rules, not magic overflow prevention.

reasoning.approach: Subtract the gap from the container width first, then divide the remaining space by the total number of fr units.
reasoning.pitfall: Using `50%` columns plus `gap: 1rem` fails because the columns alone already fill the container and the gap causes overflow.
reasoning.verify: For a 600px container with a 1rem gap at 16px, each 1fr track measures 292px in the grid inspector.

reasoning.approach: Append a fourth card element to the container and let auto placement put it into the next available cell.
reasoning.pitfall: Adding `grid-column` and `grid-row` values for each new card fails because the layout breaks when cards are added or removed.
reasoning.verify: The new card appears in the next cell with no new CSS rules, and the grid overlay shows the same tracks.

reasoning.approach: Use `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 14rem), 1fr))` with a gap, and keep the cards in reading order in the source.
reasoning.pitfall: Using `minmax(14rem, 1fr)` without `min()` fails because a container narrower than 14rem forces horizontal overflow.
reasoning.verify: In a container 12rem wide, one column fills the space and the page shows no horizontal scrollbar.

reasoning.approach: Inspect the track sizes in the grid overlay and check whether a long value set the min-content width.
reasoning.pitfall: Adding `overflow: hidden` to the cell fails because the track is still sized by content and the hidden text is lost.
reasoning.verify: After switching to `minmax(0, 1fr)` and wrapping, both tracks report equal widths in the overlay.

reasoning.approach: Render the grid with zero cards, one card and seven cards, checking both a wide and a narrow container.
reasoning.pitfall: Tuning the layout for exactly three cards fails because a seventh card leaves an awkward final row that you never saw.
reasoning.verify: The seven-card grid wraps into full rows plus one partial row, and the empty grid shows a message rather than a gap.

reasoning.approach: Compare one card in a wide container under `auto-fit` and under `auto-fill`, watching whether it stretches.
reasoning.pitfall: Treating the keywords as synonyms fails because with few items `auto-fill` keeps empty tracks and the card stays narrow.
reasoning.verify: With one card, `auto-fit` stretches it across the row, while `auto-fill` keeps it at one track width.

contrast.heading: a 1fr track widened by a long value
contrast.setup: The first rule looks equivalent to worked example 1 but omits `minmax(0, 1fr)`. Place a long URL in the first cell.
contrast.reading: A plain `1fr` track has an automatic minimum equal to its min-content size, so a long unbroken URL makes the first column wider than the second and can push the grid past its container. In `.grid-b` the minimum is 0, so both columns stay equal and the URL overflows inside its own cell, where you can add `overflow-wrap: anywhere` to keep it readable. With short words both grids look identical, which is why this difference only appears when you test with long content.

chapters.title: Responsive layouts and content-driven breakpoints
key_terms: Responsive design
Building one page that adapts its layout to the available space instead of making separate pages for each device.
Viewport meta element
The `meta name="viewport"` element that tells mobile browsers to lay out at the device width rather than a wide virtual page.
Media query
An `@media` condition, such as a minimum width, that applies rules only when the environment matches.
Breakpoint
A width at which the layout changes, chosen where the content starts to break rather than to match a particular device.
Mobile first
Writing the narrow layout as the default and adding minimum-width media queries for wider screens.
chapters.mental:
Responsive design lets one document work across available sizes and user settings. A breakpoint is a condition where a layout needs to change, not a permanent name for a device. A phone can have a wide landscape viewport; a desktop window can be narrow. Start with content that works in a small space and add more complex arrangements only when enough room exists.

The viewport metadata tells mobile browsers to use the device's layout width rather than a historical wide page assumption. Flexible widths, wrapping and content-driven heights solve many problems before a media query is necessary. A responsive page must also survive enlarged text, translations and long values, not merely a list of screen widths.
chapters.anatomy: Use a base single-column layout and a min-width media query for a wider arrangement. Relative units in queries support a design tied to text scale. Inspect where the content becomes cramped and choose the breakpoint from that evidence. Keep the navigation visible or provide a fully accessible disclosure rather than simply hiding it on small screens.

Add a second column only when content has room.
The wider layout gives navigation a bounded column.

Read the rules outside the media query first; they are the baseline.

Choose a breakpoint by resizing actual content.
Record where labels or article width become uncomfortable rather than choosing a device name.
Resize the preview slowly and note where the content itself starts to look cramped.
Content-driven breakpoints follow the design's real limits, while device-named widths go out of date as screens change.
Build a responsive course outline with a readable article.
The page adapts between stacked and two-column layouts without losing content.
Write the single-column layout first, then add one min-width query for the side-by-side layout.
A small-screen baseline works everywhere, and the enhancement applies only when the measured space allows it.
Diagnose a mobile page rendered as a tiny desktop screenshot.
Check viewport metadata and inflexible widths.
Look for the viewport meta element and any fixed pixel widths.
Without width=device-width the mobile browser lays out a wide virtual page and scales it down, and fixed widths prevent reflow.
Test narrow width together with enlarged text.
All controls and text remain reachable with no required two-axis page scrolling.
Combine a narrow width with 200 percent text zoom.
Larger text needs more space, so a layout that fits at default size can force horizontal scrolling when zoomed.
Explain why responsive design is more than media queries.
Intrinsic sizing, wrapping, content order and user settings are fundamental parts of the behavior.
List behaviors that adapt without any media query.
Intrinsic sizing, wrapping, flexible units and source order already respond to space and user settings; media queries only adjust the remaining cases.
chapters.mistakes: Do not hide essential actions just because space is limited. Avoid fixed viewport-height panels that trap content behind mobile browser chrome. Test actual text growth and settled layout.

reasoning.approach: Read the base rule outside the media query: it sets grid with a gap but no columns, so one implicit column holds every section.
reasoning.pitfall: Predicting two columns because the stylesheet mentions them fails because that rule only applies when the `min-width` query matches.
reasoning.verify: Below 48rem wide, the grid overlay shows one column and the Styles panel shows the media rule as inactive.

reasoning.approach: Slowly narrow the preview and write down the width where labels wrap awkwardly or the article column becomes too narrow.
reasoning.pitfall: Choosing 768px because it matches a tablet fails because your content may break earlier or later than that device.
reasoning.verify: Your recorded breakpoint, converted to rem, matches the width where you saw the layout become cramped.

reasoning.approach: Write a single-column base, then add a `min-width` query that places navigation in a bounded column beside a flexible article.
reasoning.pitfall: Starting from the desktop layout and hiding parts with `max-width` queries fails because narrow screens may lose content entirely.
reasoning.verify: Below the breakpoint, navigation and article stack; above it, they sit side by side with every link still present.

reasoning.approach: Check the head for viewport metadata, then look for fixed widths such as `width: 1024px` on wrappers.
reasoning.pitfall: Adding more media queries fails when the metadata is missing, because the browser still pretends the screen is wide.
reasoning.verify: After adding viewport metadata, a phone emulation shows the base layout and `window.innerWidth` matches the device width.

reasoning.approach: Combine the narrow preset with 200 percent zoom and scroll through the page in both directions.
reasoning.pitfall: Testing narrow width at default text size fails because enlarged text often reveals fixed widths that force sideways scrolling.
reasoning.verify: At narrow width and 200 percent zoom, reading requires only vertical scrolling and every control is reachable.

reasoning.approach: List behaviors that work without any query: wrapping flex rows, `minmax` grid tracks, `max-inline-size` and user font settings.
reasoning.pitfall: Treating breakpoints as the whole design fails because between breakpoints the layout can still overflow when nothing else is intrinsic.
reasoning.verify: Remove all media queries temporarily; the page still remains readable at narrow widths, only less polished.

contrast.heading: a missing viewport meta tag
contrast.setup: The responsive CSS from both worked examples is identical in these two documents. Only the head differs.

<!-- A: no viewport metadata -->
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8" />
  <title>Outline</title>
</head>

<!-- B: layout viewport follows the device -->

Document B sets the layout viewport to the device width, so a phone stays below 48rem and gets the single-column base layout. A desktop preview resized by hand may not show this difference, so use a device emulation preset when you test it.

chapters.title: Custom properties, tokens and component themes
key_terms: Custom property
A property whose name starts with two hyphens, such as `--space-2`, read with `var()` and inherited by descendants.
Design token
A named design decision, such as a color or spacing step, defined once and reused across components.
Var fallback
The second argument of `var()`, used when the referenced custom property is not defined.
Theme
A set of token values, often scoped to a class or attribute, that changes a component's appearance without changing its rules.
chapters.mental:
A design token names a recurring design decision such as a spacing step, text color or border radius. CSS custom properties store values that participate in the cascade and can be scoped to a component. A variable name should communicate its purpose, such as --surface or --space-small, rather than merely its current value. That allows the value to change while the role remains stable.

Custom properties are resolved where they are used and usually inherit. A card can override a small set of tokens while retaining the same component rules. A fallback in var supplies a value when a variable is missing or invalid in the relevant way, but a custom property can still produce an invalid declaration at computed-value time. Test the final computed result instead of assuming any string is suitable for any property.
chapters.anatomy: Define shared defaults at :root and override them on a component class. `background:var(--surface,white)` uses the current scope's value. Keep semantic text labels independent of theme color. A theme change must preserve contrast and focus behavior, not merely update an accent swatch.

One component consumes three reusable tokens.
Only descendants of this component inherit the override.
The featured card changes without copying its full rule set.

Find which element the override is declared on and follow inheritance downward.
Custom properties inherit like normal properties, so an override applies to its element and descendants but not to siblings.
Replace repeated spacing literals with a semantic token.
A deliberate single token change updates the related spacing.
Name the spacing by its role and replace each literal with var().
A token defined once changes every use together, which keeps related spacing consistent.
Build two themed cards using one component rule.
The variants preserve content labels, contrast and focus while sharing structure.
Write one .card rule that reads tokens, then override only the tokens for the variant.
The component rule stays the same while the variant changes values, so structure, labels and focus styles are shared.
Diagnose a custom property used with an incompatible value.
Inspect the final property and computed-value validity, not only the variable's existence.
Inspect the computed value of the property that uses var().

A role name such as --error-text still makes sense after the palette changes, while --red-500 becomes misleading.
chapters.mistakes: Do not treat a token system as a substitute for a content design. Overly granular tokens can make simple changes harder. A dark theme needs a full state review, not a global invert filter.

reasoning.pitfall: Expecting sibling cards to change fails because a scoped override affects the element and its descendants, never its siblings.
reasoning.verify: Only the `.featured` card shows #e0f2fe in Computed, while the other cards still resolve `--surface` to white.

reasoning.verify: Changing `--space` to 1.25rem updates all related paddings and gaps while font sizes stay unchanged.

reasoning.approach: Write one `.card` rule that reads tokens and a variant class that only overrides tokens, keeping the HTML labels identical.
reasoning.pitfall: Copying the whole `.card` rule for the variant fails because later fixes to one rule are easily forgotten in the other.
reasoning.verify: Both cards share one rule in the Styles panel, and each variant passes a contrast check for text and focus.

reasoning.approach: Inspect the property that consumes the token in Computed and check whether the substituted value is valid for that property.
reasoning.pitfall: Checking only that `--space` is defined fails because invalid substitution makes the property unset while the variable looks fine.
reasoning.verify: The Computed panel reports the expected padding after you correct the token to a length.

reasoning.approach: Delete the optional token's definition and confirm the fallback in `var(--surface, white)` takes over.

reasoning.verify: With the token removed, the card background computes to white and the text remains readable.

reasoning.approach: Name tokens for the role they play, such as `--error-text`, rather than the specific hue currently assigned.

contrast.heading: a token holding the wrong kind of value
contrast.setup: Custom properties accept almost anything, so the error appears only where the token is used. Inspect the card's padding.

The Computed panel shows padding 0px while `--space` still appears as a defined variable, which is why checking that the token exists is not enough.

chapters.title: Pseudo-classes, pseudo-elements and stateful styling
key_terms: Pseudo-class
A selector keyword after one colon, such as `:hover` or `:checked`, that matches elements by state or position.
Pseudo-element
A selector after two colons, such as `::before`, that styles part of an element or content generated for it.
Attribute selector
A selector such as `[aria-current="page"]` that matches elements by the presence or value of an attribute.
Focus-within
The `:focus-within` pseudo-class, which matches an element when it or any descendant has focus.
User-invalid
The `:user-invalid` pseudo-class, which matches an invalid control only after the user has interacted with it.
chapters.mental:
A pseudo-class selects an element based on a condition such as focus, checked state or its position among siblings. A pseudo-element represents a stylable part associated with an element, such as before or after. Generated decorative content can enrich presentation, but essential instructions should exist as real document content because generated content has inconsistent accessibility implications.

State should remain grounded in a real control or application contract. Styling a checkbox's checked state makes use of built-in behavior. A decorative class named active does not prove that a control is selected, and CSS cannot perform server authorization. Use native state first and add custom state only with a clear interaction model.
chapters.anatomy: `:focus-within` matches a container while one of its descendants has focus. `input:checked + span` selects a neighboring label fragment after a checked input. Attribute selectors can target a declared state, but the application is responsible for keeping that state accurate. `:has()` selects an element by what it contains, so `.field:has(input:user-invalid)` styles a whole field group when its input is invalid. `:user-invalid` matches only after the person has interacted with the control, unlike `:invalid`, which also matches an untouched required field on page load. `:is()` takes the specificity of its most specific argument, while `:where()` always contributes zero specificity, which makes it useful for easily overridden defaults. Hover must be an enhancement because touch and keyboard interactions may not provide the same hover behavior.

The container helps the user locate the current task and shows an error only after interaction.
The field group changes while its descendant is focused, and turns to the error color only after the user has left the input in an invalid state.
The checkbox remains the actual control.

Operate the controls without hover.
All actions and state information remain usable by keyboard and touch.
Use only Tab, Space and Enter, then try a touch screen without hover.
Hover is unavailable on touch and keyboard, so anything shown only on hover is lost to those users.
Explain why CSS state cannot authorize a server action.
Presentation can be changed by the client; the server must enforce permission using trusted context.
Ask who controls the CSS once the page reaches the browser.
Users can change styles and requests freely, so permission decisions must use trusted server-side identity and data.
chapters.mistakes: A hover-only menu can exclude keyboard users. Generated text can be skipped or announced unexpectedly. Keep meaningful text in the document and let CSS reinforce it.

reasoning.approach: Ask whether the selector matches an element in a state, such as `:checked`, or creates a stylable part, such as `::before`.
reasoning.pitfall: Calling `::before` a state fails because it never matches a condition; it creates a box that exists only for presentation.
reasoning.verify: The Elements panel shows `::before` as a pseudo node inside the element, while `:checked` appears only as a matched selector.

reasoning.approach: Wrap the label and input in a `.field` container and add a `:focus-within` border color to that container.
reasoning.pitfall: Using `.field:focus` fails because the container itself never receives focus, so the rule never matches.
reasoning.verify: Tab into the input and the field border changes; tab out and the border returns to its default.

reasoning.approach: Use native checkboxes inside labels and style `input:checked + span` so text weight reinforces the checked state.
reasoning.pitfall: Building toggles from `span` elements with a `selected` class fails because no state reaches assistive technology or keyboard users.
reasoning.verify: Pressing Space on a focused checkbox toggles it, its accessible state changes, and the adjacent text becomes bold.

reasoning.approach: Move the instruction text into a real element in HTML and connect it to the field with `aria-describedby`.
reasoning.pitfall: Adding `aria-label` to the pseudo element fails because pseudo elements are not DOM nodes and cannot carry attributes.
reasoning.verify: Selecting all text on the page now includes the instruction, and the input's description lists it.

reasoning.approach: Disconnect the mouse mentally: reach every control with Tab, toggle with Space or Enter, and read each state without hovering.
reasoning.pitfall: Revealing state only on `:hover` fails because keyboard and touch users never trigger hover in a dependable way.
reasoning.verify: Every state label is visible without hovering, and each action is completed using only the keyboard.

reasoning.approach: Note that any CSS state can be changed in developer tools, so permission must be checked by the server using its own session.
reasoning.pitfall: Hiding an admin button with `display: none` fails because the endpoint still accepts a request sent directly.
reasoning.verify: Unhiding the button in developer tools shows it again, proving the style held no security decision.

contrast.heading: an instruction that exists only in generated content
contrast.setup: Both fields look the same on screen. Copy the page text and inspect the accessibility tree for each one.
contrast.code: Use your student number.
contrast.reading: The first instruction is painted by `::before`, so it does not exist in the DOM text. Copying the page omits it, some assistive technology announces it inconsistently, and if the stylesheet fails to load the instruction disappears. The second is a real paragraph that also becomes the input's description through `aria-describedby`. Keep generated content for decoration such as icons or separators, and put anything a person must read into HTML.

chapters.title: Transitions, motion and reduced-motion preferences
key_terms: Transition
An interpolation from an old to a new property value over a set duration when the value changes, such as on hover.
Transform
The property that moves, scales or rotates a box visually without changing the layout of its neighbors.
Keyframes animation
An `@keyframes` rule naming intermediate states, run with the `animation` property without needing a state change.
Reduced motion preference
The `prefers-reduced-motion` media feature, which reports that a user asked the system to minimize nonessential motion.
chapters.mental:
Motion can explain a change, but it can also distract, delay a task or cause discomfort. A transition interpolates between property values when state changes. An animation uses named keyframes over time. Neither should be required to understand essential content. Begin with the static usable state and add restrained motion only when it improves orientation.

Animating layout-affecting properties can trigger repeated layout work, while transform and opacity often allow more efficient compositing. This is not a guarantee of smooth performance because element size, painting and the device still matter. Measure actual behavior rather than assuming that a property name proves efficiency. Continuous decorative motion rarely helps a reading task.
chapters.anatomy: Specify the properties to transition instead of transition:all, which can animate unrelated future changes. The prefers-reduced-motion media query lets a page respond to a user's preference. A reduced-motion rule can remove movement while retaining a color or outline change. Do not use a tiny but nonzero duration as a universal accessibility strategy; understand the interaction's required events and states.
examples: Only the intended visual property is animated.
Pointer hover produces a small positional cue.
The static state stays fully usable.
The positional motion is removed for the reduced-motion preference.
tasks: Identify the difference between a transition and keyframe animation.
A transition follows a property change; an animation follows a named timeline.
Ask what starts each one: a property change or a named sequence.
A transition interpolates between two values when a property changes, while @keyframes define a timeline that runs on its own.
Limit a transition to one intentional property.
Unrelated style changes no longer animate automatically.
Name the property in transition instead of using all.
transition: all animates every later property change, including ones you did not intend; listing one property keeps the effect deliberate.
Build a card interaction with a static reduced-motion alternative.
The card remains understandable and usable without movement.
Write the static version first, then add motion only outside prefers-reduced-motion: reduce.
The reduced-motion query lets people who are sensitive to motion get a fully usable static interaction.
Diagnose an animation that hides information until it finishes.
Make the essential content available without waiting for motion.
Check whether the content is readable before the animation ends.
Information that appears only at the end of an animation delays or hides it for everyone and fails when motion is disabled.
Test with reduced motion enabled and with keyboard focus.
Motion is reduced and the focus indicator still communicates interaction.
Turn on the operating system's reduce-motion setting and tab to the card.
Disabling motion must not remove the focus indicator, which communicates state rather than decoration.
Explain why transform does not guarantee a fast page.
The full rendering workload, content size and device determine performance.
Profile a page with many large elements that animate at the same time.
transform avoids layout but still costs painting and compositing, so total workload and device speed decide performance.
chapters.mistakes: Do not make reduced motion disable the action itself. Avoid infinite animations in reading material. Test the preference in a real browser because source presence does not prove the rule won the cascade.

reasoning.approach: Compare triggers: a transition runs only when a property value changes, while a keyframe animation runs from its own named timeline.
reasoning.pitfall: Expecting a transition to loop fails because it runs once per value change and stops at the new value.
reasoning.verify: A hover transition plays once per hover and then rests, while an `animation` with `animation-iteration-count: infinite` keeps running with no interaction at all.

reasoning.approach: Replace `transition: all` with `transition: transform 120ms ease` so only the intended movement animates.
reasoning.pitfall: Keeping `all` with a shorter duration fails because unrelated layout changes still animate, just more quickly.
reasoning.verify: Changing the card's padding in developer tools happens instantly while hover still animates the transform.

reasoning.approach: Add the hover transform and a reduced-motion media query that removes both the transition and the transform.
reasoning.pitfall: Removing only the transition fails because the card still jumps 2px on hover, which is still motion.
reasoning.verify: With reduced motion emulated, hovering leaves the card in place and its border or outline still changes.

reasoning.approach: Make the content visible in its final state by default and let motion only decorate that change.
reasoning.pitfall: Starting content at `opacity: 0` until an animation finishes fails because a failed or skipped animation leaves the text invisible.
reasoning.verify: With animations disabled in developer tools, or with the keyframes rule deleted, all text is visible and readable as soon as the page loads.

reasoning.approach: Emulate `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`, then tab through the cards and confirm each focus outline is still visible.
reasoning.pitfall: Disabling all hover and focus styles under reduced motion fails because users lose the focus signal along with the motion.
reasoning.verify: With the preference on, no element moves and every focused card still shows its outline.

reasoning.approach: Profile a hover on a page with many large cards and look at layout, paint and composite work in the performance panel.
reasoning.pitfall: Assuming transform is free fails because large layers, many elements and slow devices still cost memory and frame time.
reasoning.verify: The performance trace shows frame timings for the hover on each version, and you compare those recorded numbers instead of assuming which one is faster.

contrast.heading: transition all animating an unrelated change
contrast.setup: A later stylesheet change makes the card wider on large screens. Compare what each transition rule does when the media query starts matching.
contrast.reading: When the viewport crosses 48rem, `.card-a` animates its padding over 400ms because `all` includes every animatable property, so text visibly slides and reflows while the reader is trying to look at it. `.card-b` jumps to the new padding at once and only animates `transform` for the hover cue. The same surprise happens with color, border or height changes added months later. Listing the intended property keeps future changes instant unless you choose to animate them.

chapters.title: Container queries and reusable responsive components
key_terms: Container query
An `@container` rule that applies styles based on the size of an ancestor container rather than the viewport.
Query container
An ancestor with `container-type` set, such as `inline-size`, whose dimensions container queries measure.
Size containment
The isolation `container-type: inline-size` applies so the container's inline size does not depend on its children, preventing a query loop.
Inline size
The dimension along the direction text runs, which is the width in a horizontal writing mode.
chapters.mental:
A media query responds to the viewport or device environment. A container query can respond to an ancestor container's size, which is useful when the same component appears in a wide article and a narrow sidebar on the same page. The component should adapt to the space it receives instead of assuming it always spans the viewport.

Size containment changes how a container participates in sizing. Declare it deliberately on an appropriate wrapper, not on every element. A size query targets an eligible ancestor, not the queried element itself. Keep a useful base layout so the component remains readable in environments where the query is unsupported or never matches.
chapters.anatomy: Set `container-type:inline-size` on a wrapper, optionally with a container-name. Inside `@container`, adjust the descendant component when its wrapper is wide enough. Prefer logical dimensions so the design does not unnecessarily assume a writing direction. This chapter demonstrates progressive enhancement; the unqueried stacked card remains functional.
examples: The wrapper supplies the size context.
The card has a usable stacked baseline.
The component's parent width matters, not the page width alone.
Only cards in sufficiently wide containers switch layout.
tasks: Explain why two cards on the same viewport can use different layouts.
Their query containers can have different widths.
Compare the widths of the two slot containers, not the viewport.
Container queries test the nearest query container, so the same component can match in one slot and not in another.
Add a container wrapper around a reusable card.
The card has an explicit local sizing context.
Set container-type: inline-size on the wrapper, not on the card.
An element cannot query its own size, so the wrapper must establish the container that the card's rules test.
Render the same component in wide and narrow slots.
Each instance adapts independently while preserving its content.
Place the same card in a wide slot and a narrow slot side by side.
Each instance evaluates the query against its own container, so they adapt independently.
Diagnose a query that never matches because no ancestor is eligible.
Inspect container-type and the relevant ancestor relationship.
Check every ancestor for container-type.
A container query only matches when an ancestor establishes size containment; without one, the query never applies.
Disable the query and inspect the fallback.
The baseline stacked component remains usable.
Remove the @container rule and check the stacked layout.
The baseline rules outside the query must work on their own, because the query is an enhancement.
Choose between a viewport query and a container query for a sidebar card.
A container query fits a component whose available space depends on placement.
Ask whether the card's space depends on the screen or on where it is placed.
A card in a sidebar gets the sidebar's width, so a container query describes its real space better than the viewport.
chapters.mistakes: Containment is not merely a label; it affects sizing behavior. Avoid a component design that becomes unusable unless a modern feature matches. Verify both instances after actual resizing.

reasoning.approach: Identify the query container for each card and compare the inline size of those two wrappers, not the width of the browser window.
reasoning.pitfall: Saying both cards must match because they share one viewport fails, since `@container` never reads the viewport width at all.
reasoning.verify: Inspect each `.slot`; the wider one shows a matched container rule while the narrower one shows the same rule unmatched.

reasoning.approach: Wrap the card in an element such as `.slot`, give that wrapper `container-type: inline-size`, and keep the card's own grid rule as the stacked baseline.
reasoning.pitfall: Adding `container-type` to the card itself fails because a query only looks at ancestors, so the card cannot change its own columns.
reasoning.verify: The Elements panel shows a container badge on `.slot`, and the card becomes a descendant of that badge.

reasoning.approach: Place one slot in a wide main column and one in a narrow sidebar, using the same card markup and a single `@container` rule.
reasoning.pitfall: Writing separate classes such as `.card-wide` and `.card-narrow` fails because each placement then needs manual edits whenever the layout around it changes.
reasoning.verify: Narrow the main column until it crosses 28rem and only that card switches layout while the sidebar card stays stacked.

reasoning.approach: Walk up from the card to the first ancestor with a non-normal `container-type` and confirm the query condition uses an axis it contains.
reasoning.pitfall: Using a `block-size` condition with `container-type: inline-size` fails because that container only exposes its inline dimension to queries.
reasoning.verify: After adding containment to the right ancestor, the Styles panel lists the container rule as matched at the wide size.

reasoning.approach: Comment out the whole `@container` block and read the card at wide and narrow widths with only the baseline grid rule active.
reasoning.pitfall: Hiding the image or text by default and revealing it in the query fails because readers lose content wherever the query does not match.
reasoning.verify: Without the query, the image, heading and text all appear in one readable stacked column at every width.

reasoning.approach: Decide which measurement controls the card: the window for page-level structure, or the slot the card happens to occupy for a reusable component.
reasoning.pitfall: Using a viewport breakpoint for the sidebar card fails because a wide screen can still give the sidebar too little room for two columns.
reasoning.verify: On a wide screen with a narrow sidebar, the container version stays stacked while a viewport version would squeeze two columns.

contrast.heading: a component that tries to query itself
contrast.setup: Here the containment declaration moved from the wrapper onto the card. The query text is unchanged from worked example 2.
contrast.reading: A container query selects the nearest ancestor that is a query container, never the element being styled. Because `.card` is now the container and no ancestor is, the `@container` rule finds nothing to measure for `.card` and the card stays stacked at every width. Children of the card could respond to its size, but the card itself cannot. Put the declaration back on `.slot`, keep the card as a descendant, and the two slots from worked example 2 again choose their layouts independently. The Styles panel marks the container rule as not applied while it is broken.

chapters.title: CSS architecture, layers and maintainable components
key_terms: Cascade layer
A named `@layer` group of rules; for normal declarations, a later layer wins over an earlier one regardless of specificity.
Unlayered declaration
A normal declaration outside every layer, which takes priority over all layered normal declarations.
Utility
A narrowly named single-purpose class for a deliberate local adjustment, usually placed in the last layer.
Native CSS nesting
Writing a rule inside its parent rule, where `&` stands for the parent selector, such as `&:hover`.
Where pseudo-class
The `:where()` wrapper, which gives its selector zero specificity so later rules can override it easily.
chapters.mental:
A stylesheet is easier to change when responsibilities are visible. Base rules describe document defaults, component rules describe reusable structures, and narrowly named utilities make deliberate local adjustments. These categories are a design choice, not a browser feature by themselves. Cascade layers let authors establish an explicit ordering among groups of declarations without continually increasing selector specificity.

For normal author declarations, later layers take priority over earlier layers, and unlayered normal declarations have priority over layered normal declarations. Important declarations reverse layer priority, which is one reason indiscriminate important usage makes reasoning harder. A good architecture keeps selectors understandable and limits the area a change can affect.
chapters.anatomy: Declare the layer order once with `@layer base, components, utilities`. Put actual rules inside those layers. Native CSS nesting keeps a component's states next to its base rule: inside `.note { ... }`, the nested `&:hover { ... }` means `.note:hover`. Wrapping a selector in `:where()` sets its specificity to zero, so `:where(.note) a` is easy for a later component or utility rule to override. Keep component names tied to a useful responsibility such as lesson-card, not a visual accident such as left-blue-box. Test a component in more than one surrounding context to expose accidental ancestor dependencies.
examples: Layer order establishes a policy before selectors compete within it.
The component layer can override the earlier base rule, and the nested &:hover rule applies to .note:hover inside the same layer.
The utility overrides earlier normal layered color declarations.
tasks: Predict the layer winner for normal declarations.
A later declared layer outranks an earlier one before specificity is compared.
Read the @layer order statement first, then compare which layer each rule is in.
For normal declarations, a later layer beats an earlier one regardless of selector specificity.
Move a component's rules into one named layer.
Its styling responsibility is grouped and discoverable.
Wrap all of the component's rules in one @layer components block.
Grouping the rules by responsibility makes their priority predictable and easy to find.
Build a small layered stylesheet with base, component and utility rules.
The intended overrides work without escalating ids or important flags.
Declare the three layers once at the top, then fill each layer with simple selectors.
Layer order resolves conflicts, so you do not need ids or !important to make a utility win.
Diagnose an unlayered rule unexpectedly beating layered normal rules.
Unlayered normal author declarations have higher layer priority.
Find rules that are outside every @layer block.
Unlayered normal declarations beat all layered normal declarations, which surprises authors who expect source order to decide.
Place the component under a different parent.
Its behavior does not rely on an accidental deep ancestor selector.
Move the component into another parent and see whether its styles still apply.
A selector tied to a deep ancestor chain breaks when the component moves, while a component class keeps working.
Explain why important declarations complicate layer reasoning.
Important layer ordering is reversed, so the normal ordering intuition no longer applies.
Mark one declaration !important in an early layer and predict the result.
For important declarations the layer order reverses, so an earlier layer wins, the opposite of normal declarations.
chapters.mistakes: A named architecture cannot prevent global selectors from leaking. Do not put every exception in an unlayered file because that silently bypasses the policy. Keep examples small enough to trace.

reasoning.approach: Compare the layer order declared in the first `@layer` statement first, and only compare specificity for declarations that share a layer.
reasoning.pitfall: Choosing the rule with the more specific selector fails because a later layer wins over an earlier one no matter how specific the earlier selector is.
reasoning.verify: Give the base rule an id selector; the component color still wins, and the Styles panel strikes through the base declaration.

reasoning.approach: Gather the `.note` rule and its nested `&:hover` state into one `@layer components` block and delete the scattered copies.
reasoning.pitfall: Leaving the hover rule unlayered at the bottom of the file fails because it now outranks utilities and becomes impossible to override cleanly.
reasoning.verify: Searching the stylesheet for `.note` finds one block, and hovering a note still underlines it.

reasoning.approach: Declare the order once, put element defaults in base, components in components, and single-purpose helpers such as `.text-muted` in utilities.
reasoning.pitfall: Fixing an override by adding `!important` to a utility fails because important declarations reverse layer order and make later reasoning harder.
reasoning.verify: Adding `.text-muted` to a note changes its color to #475569 with no `!important` and no id selector anywhere.

reasoning.approach: Search the stylesheet for rules outside any `@layer` block, especially late quick fixes, and move each into the layer that matches its role.
reasoning.pitfall: Raising the component selector's specificity fails because the unlayered rule wins before specificity is even compared.
reasoning.verify: Once the quick fix lives in base, the component color appears and the Styles panel shows the unlayered rule gone.

reasoning.approach: Move the card's markup from the main column into an aside and check that every component style still applies in the new place.
reasoning.pitfall: Writing selectors like `main section .card p` fails because the component then loses its styles the moment it moves outside that ancestry.
reasoning.verify: The card renders identically inside the aside, and its matched rules list only component class selectors.

reasoning.approach: Recall that for important declarations the layer ranking flips, so an earlier layer's `!important` beats a later layer's `!important`.
reasoning.pitfall: Assuming important rules simply follow the normal later-wins order fails because base `!important` would then be expected to lose, which it does not.
reasoning.verify: Mark the same property important in base and utilities; the base value wins, which matches the reversed order.

contrast.heading: an unlayered selector beating a layered component
contrast.setup: Someone adds a quick fix outside every layer. Predict the color of `.note` paragraphs before inspecting.
contrast.reading: For normal declarations, unlayered author styles rank above every named layer, and layer order is compared before specificity. The class selector `.note` is more specific than the type selector `p`, but that comparison never happens: the unlayered `p` rule wins, so note paragraphs turn #172033. Moving the quick fix into `@layer base` restores the intended outcome, because base is declared first and components now outranks it. The Styles panel lists the losing `.note` declaration as struck through, which is the evidence to look for.

chapters.title: Print styles, progressive enhancement and resilient delivery
key_terms: Print stylesheet
Rules inside `@media print` that adapt a page for paper, such as hiding navigation and avoiding awkward page breaks.
Progressive enhancement
Starting from a working HTML baseline and adding CSS and script features only where the browser supports them.
Feature query
An `@supports` rule that applies its styles only when the browser supports the stated property and value.
Fallback
A simpler declaration or layout that remains usable when an enhancement is unsupported or fails to load.
chapters.mental:
Progressive enhancement starts from useful content and adds capabilities when the environment supports them. A document should communicate its core information before advanced styling or scripts run. This does not mean every application must offer identical features in every environment; it means essential requirements and fallbacks are deliberate rather than accidental.

Print is a different presentation context. Navigation controls that are useful on screen can waste space on paper, while a visible URL or document title may become more valuable. A print stylesheet can remove decoration, preserve contrast and avoid splitting small related blocks. It cannot guarantee the printer, paper size or user settings, so inspect the browser's print preview before making claims.
chapters.anatomy: Use `@media print` for print-specific rules and `@supports` for a feature-dependent enhancement. Keep the base rule valid independently. Avoid hiding the actual article while removing navigation. `break-inside:avoid` is a request to the fragmentation system, not a promise that an arbitrarily large element fits on one page.
examples: Hide actions while retaining the document.
The article remains while interactive controls are removed.
The fallback remains a readable block layout.
Supported environments use Grid; others keep the content.
tasks: Identify content that must survive when scripts fail.
The page's primary information and basic navigation remain available.
Disable JavaScript and list what is still readable and navigable.
Content and links in the HTML remain available when scripts fail, which is the baseline progressive enhancement protects.
Add a print rule that removes only irrelevant controls.
The article and its headings remain in print preview.
Hide only navigation and buttons inside @media print.
A print view keeps the article and headings because the reader wants the content, not controls that cannot work on paper.
Build printable study notes with a useful baseline layout.
Screen and print views preserve meaning with appropriate presentation.
Start from a single-column readable baseline, then add print and screen adjustments.
A content-first baseline keeps meaning in both media, while each media query only changes presentation.
Diagnose a print rule that hides the main region.
Narrow the selector to navigation or actions instead of the content container.
Check whether the print selector matches the main element or one of its ancestors.
display: none on a container removes everything inside it, so the rule must target the controls themselves.
Inspect multiple pages of print preview.
Headings, tables and long blocks remain legible across page breaks.
Open print preview and scroll through every page.
Page breaks can split tables and headings from their content, which only appears across multiple pages.
Explain what a feature query proves and what it does not.
It detects supported syntax, not performance, usability or correctness of the whole component.
Ask what @supports actually tests.
A feature query checks whether the browser parses a property and value, not whether the result is fast, accessible or correct.
chapters.mistakes: Do not confuse feature detection with browser sniffing. Avoid claiming print quality from a screen screenshot. A large table may need its own print strategy rather than an indiscriminate no-break rule.

reasoning.approach: List what a reader came for, such as the article text, headings and plain links, and mark which pieces must work without scripts or styles.
reasoning.pitfall: Naming the animated menu or the filter widget as essential fails because those enhancements depend on scripts that may never run.
reasoning.verify: Disable JavaScript in developer tools; the article and its links are still present and readable in order.

reasoning.approach: Inside `@media print`, hide only `nav` and `button`, and reset the body to black text on a white background.
reasoning.pitfall: Hiding a wrapper that contains both navigation and the article fails because the descendants, including the content, disappear in print as well.
reasoning.verify: Print preview shows the article heading and paragraphs while navigation and buttons are gone.

reasoning.approach: Start from a block baseline for notes, add a Grid layout inside `@supports (display: grid)`, then add a print rule that removes controls only.
reasoning.pitfall: Putting the only layout inside the `@supports` block with no block baseline fails because unsupported environments get no readable structure at all.
reasoning.verify: Removing the `@supports` block leaves notes readable in one column, and print preview keeps every heading.

reasoning.approach: Inspect which element the print selector matches and check whether the main content is its descendant.
reasoning.pitfall: Adding `display: block` to `main` inside the print rule fails because a hidden ancestor still hides every child.
reasoning.verify: After narrowing the selector to `nav`, print preview shows the main region on the first page.

reasoning.approach: Scroll through every page of print preview and read the headings, table rows and long code blocks at each page break.
reasoning.pitfall: Applying `break-inside: avoid` to the whole article fails because an element taller than a page must still split somewhere.
reasoning.verify: Each page starts with readable content, and no heading sits alone at the bottom of a page.

reasoning.approach: Read the `@supports` condition as a parser check: the browser reports whether it understands that property and value pair.
reasoning.pitfall: Treating a matched feature query as proof that the layout works well fails because supported syntax can still overflow or misorder content.
reasoning.verify: A grid inside a matched `@supports` block can still overflow at narrow width, which you see only by resizing.

contrast.heading: a print rule that hides the article
contrast.setup: The page wraps navigation and content in one `.shell` element. Compare two print rules written to remove the menu.
contrast.reading: The first rule removes the wrapper, and `display: none` takes every descendant with it, so print preview shows a blank page or only the footer even though the screen view looks perfect. The second rule names the navigation and the buttons, leaving `main` and its headings in place. Screen rendering is identical for both versions, because neither rule applies outside print media. Only opening print preview reveals the difference, which is why the guide asks you to inspect preview pages rather than the screen.

chapters.title: HTML and CSS milestone: an accessible learning portal
key_terms: Information architecture
The organization, labeling and navigation of content, so readers can find and understand what they need.
Component system
A set of reusable patterns, such as a card or button, built from shared tokens with documented states.
Responsive audit
A check of a page at several widths and zoom levels that records any overflow, reading order or focus problem.
Acceptance criteria
Concrete, testable conditions that a page or feature must meet before it counts as done.
chapters.mental:
A portal combines structure, navigation and repeated components around a user goal. Begin with the tasks: finding a topic, understanding prerequisites, choosing an action and reading progress. The information architecture groups content so those tasks are discoverable. A beautiful collection of cards is not enough if every label is vague or the reading order hides the main choice.

This milestone integrates the earlier mechanisms without requiring a framework. Semantic headings establish the outline, native links provide navigation, Grid or Flexbox distributes cards, and tokens maintain consistent spacing and color. Progress labels remain textual. The project uses synthetic data and does not claim persistent accounts or a working backend.
chapters.anatomy: Write acceptance criteria before styling: one main region, descriptive page title, reachable navigation, distinct card headings, no color-only status, a narrow-width layout and a usable zoomed view. Implement the smallest coherent page, then audit the settled state at multiple widths. Keep appearance checks separate from structural checks because each can pass while the other fails.
examples: The heading and link describe the same destination.

HTML foundations

Beginner. No prerequisites.

Read HTML foundations
A reader knows the topic, entry requirement and next action.
The layout supports a changing number of topics.
tasks: Write three learner tasks before drawing the interface.
Find a topic, assess its prerequisites and choose a clear next action.
Describe what a learner needs to do before choosing any layout.
Starting from tasks keeps the interface focused on finding a topic, checking prerequisites and taking the next step.
Define a small token set for the page.
Spacing, text and surface choices are consistent and named by role.
Limit the tokens to surface, text, accent and spacing, named by role.
A small role-based token set keeps the page consistent and makes later palette changes safe.
Build a complete offline portal with three paths and local destinations.
All cards, navigation and headings are meaningful, keyboard reachable and responsive.
Build the HTML structure first, then layer the CSS on top of it.
A meaningful structure keeps the portal usable without styles, and the CSS then adapts it to different widths.
Audit one deliberately vague link and one broken fragment.
Replace the vague label and repair the target relationship.
Read each link out of context and click every fragment link.
Link text must describe its destination, and every fragment must match an existing id.
Review narrow width, zoom, keyboard and print behavior.
Retain observations for each surface instead of claiming a universal pass from one screenshot.
Record one observation for each surface instead of a single screenshot.
Narrow width, zoom, keyboard and print each exercise different behavior, so each needs its own evidence.
Explain the portal's remaining backend requirements.

chapters.title: Connect HTML to JavaScript: DOM, events and safe text
key_terms: DOM
The Document Object Model, the live tree of objects the browser builds from HTML, which scripts can read and change.
Event listener
A function registered with `addEventListener` that runs when a named event, such as `click`, reaches an element.
TextContent
The `textContent` property, which reads or sets an element's text without parsing it as HTML, so data cannot become markup.
State
The data a script keeps about the interface, such as a count or a selected item, from which the display is drawn.
Deferred script
A script marked `defer`, or a module script, that runs after the document is parsed, so the elements it needs already exist.
chapters.mental:
The document object model is the browser's live tree of elements. JavaScript can select a node, observe an event and update content. HTML supplies the structure, CSS supplies presentation, and JavaScript handles behavior. Start with a native button so keyboard activation and focus work without reimplementation. The event listener is a function called when a matching event occurs; it is not the same as calling the function immediately while registering it.

Keep state separate from the text that displays it. A numeric count in a variable is the source of truth; a render function translates it into a label. Reading the current label and repeatedly parsing it back into a number couples business state to presentation. Use textContent for plain user text because it creates text rather than parsing markup.
chapters.anatomy:
`document.querySelector('#add')` returns a matching element or null. `addEventListener('click', handler)` registers a function. Update the number, then render the new value to an output element. Query elements after they exist, for example with a script at the end of the body. For JavaScript syntax, revisit the JavaScript foundations and browser chapters rather than treating this lesson as a substitute for that route.

A classic inline script runs when the parser reaches it. A script in the head cannot assume that later body elements already exist. Separate classic script tags share the document's global lexical environment, while a module has its own scope and strict semantics. DOMContentLoaded fires after parsing and the relevant deferred script work; it does not mean every image has loaded. The load event describes the later document load boundary. Register a listener before its event occurs, or inspect readyState when code can be loaded at different times.

An external classic script with defer preserves document order and waits for parsing. Async scripts do not provide that same ordering guarantee. Defer does not turn an inline classic script into a deferred one. Inline modules use real module semantics, including top-level this being undefined. The classroom supports inline modules but blocks external script files and imports. Study multi-file loading in a separately prepared local project rather than weakening the preview policy.
examples: A name is data even when it contains angle brackets.
The literal name appears as text, not a new HTML element.
The state is numeric and independent of its label.

tasks: Predict when the registered callback executes.
It runs on a matching event, not merely because the listener was registered.
Separate registering the listener from the moment the user clicks.

Use native buttons for increment and reset, and an output element for the result.
Native buttons are keyboard operable, and output can be announced as a status when its text changes.

Inspect the document relationship before attaching the listener.

querySelector returns null when no element matches, and calling a method on null throws a TypeError.
Insert text containing angle brackets without creating markup.
textContent preserves the literal data and creates no extra element.
Use textContent rather than innerHTML for the inserted string.
textContent stores characters as text, so angle brackets never reach the HTML parser and cannot create elements.
Explain why reading state back from formatted text is fragile.
Formatting, localization and extra words can break parsing while the underlying number is unchanged.
Change the displayed wording and see whether reading the number back still works.
Parsing formatted text couples logic to presentation, so a translation or extra word breaks the state.
chapters.mistakes: Do not invoke handler() when you meant to pass handler to the listener. Avoid using innerHTML for plain labels. A programmatic click checks logic but does not replace a keyboard interaction test.

chapters.title: Disclosures, dialogs and focus management
key_terms: Disclosure
A control that shows or hides content in the current document, provided natively by `details` and `summary`.
Modal dialog
A `dialog` opened with `showModal()` that makes the rest of the page inert until it closes.
Focus restoration
Returning keyboard focus to the control that opened a dialog when it closes, if that control still exists.
Native control
A built-in element such as `button` or `details` that already supplies keyboard behavior and accessible semantics.
chapters.mental:
A disclosure reveals content in the current document, while a dialog creates a focused interaction context. These are different patterns and should not be chosen only for visual style. Native details and summary elements provide a useful disclosure without JavaScript. A modal dialog changes which content can be interacted with and needs a clear way to close, an accessible name and sensible focus restoration.

Focus is part of the interaction's state. When a dialog opens, the user should land in a meaningful place. When it closes, focus usually returns to the control that opened it if that control still exists. Keyboard users must not become trapped in an accidental custom implementation. Native dialog behavior supplies important mechanics, but authors still own labeling, content order and testing.
chapters.anatomy: Use details with summary for optional explanation. Use a dialog element and showModal when a true modal task is justified. A form with method=dialog can close the dialog; this local behavior is distinct from a network form submission. The offline preview may restrict submission APIs, so this reference closes explicitly through the dialog API and keeps all state local.

Build a disclosure and a deliberately opened local dialog.

Native details and dialog elements provide keyboard support, Escape handling and the top layer without custom focus code.

chapters.mistakes: Do not build a dialog by merely positioning a div over the page. Avoid automatically opening modal explanations during reading. Browser behavior must be tested after interaction, not only from initial DOM structure.

chapters.title: Accessible form feedback with a pure validation function
key_terms: Validation function
A function that receives field values and returns a list of errors, kept separate from the code that updates the page.
Pure function
A function whose result depends only on its arguments and that changes nothing outside itself, which makes it easy to test.
Error summary
A list near the top of a form that names each error and links to its field, announced after a failed submission.
Aria-invalid
The `aria-invalid` attribute, which tells assistive technology that a control's current value failed validation.
chapters.mental:
Validation becomes easier to test when a pure function receives data and returns errors without touching the document. The browser layer then displays those errors and moves focus only when it helps recovery. This separation lets the same input contract be tested with normal, missing and boundary values before considering visual presentation. It does not remove the need for backend validation.

An error summary gives a user an overview after an attempted action. Field-level messages explain how to repair specific values. Connect those messages to controls and preserve entered values. Avoid announcing a long stream of errors on every keystroke. The timing of feedback is a product decision that should reduce confusion rather than punish incomplete typing.
chapters.anatomy: The reference uses a button to validate local values without submitting a form. Convert the input string carefully: trim it, reject an empty string and require digits only before calling Number, because Number also accepts 0x1e (30), 1e2 (100), 0b111 (7) and 7.5, which the server rule in web-047 rejects. Return an error list, then render it with textContent. Set aria-invalid only after a failed check. A valid result is a local observation, not a stored request.

The visible and semantic error states agree.

Use a stable message id and aria-describedby on the input.
Give the message element an id and add it to the input's aria-describedby.
aria-describedby makes the message part of the input's accessible description, so it is announced with the field.
Test empty, whitespace, negative, nonnumeric, hexadecimal (0x1e), exponent (1e2), fractional (7.5) and valid values.
Each produces the declared result with no uncaught exception.

reasoning.verify: Enter 200, validate, and see the message beside the field while 200 is still in the input.

reasoning.approach: Give the error element a stable `id` and add that `id` to the input's `aria-describedby` attribute.
reasoning.pitfall: Placing the message near the field with only CSS proximity fails because assistive technology does not link nearby text to the input.

reasoning.approach: Run each listed input through `validate` in a table and record the exact returned string next to the expected one.

chapters.title: Data interfaces: filtering tables and honest visual summaries
key_terms: Derived data
Values computed from the source data, such as a filtered list or a total, recalculated rather than stored separately.
Filter
An operation that keeps only the items matching a condition without changing the original collection.
Empty state
The message shown when a filter returns no items, explaining why and what the reader can change.
Visual encoding
The mapping from data values to visual properties such as bar length, which must be proportional and labeled honestly.
chapters.mental:
A data interface connects records to a representation. Keep the original records separate from the filtered view so a user can clear a filter without reconstructing lost input. A table is useful for exact values; a chart emphasizes patterns. Both need labels, units and a declared handling of missing values. A visually impressive chart can still tell an incorrect story if its filtering or scale is wrong.

This lesson uses a tiny local array and a semantic table. A select changes the derived records, then one render function replaces the table body with safely created cells. An empty result receives an explicit message rather than an unexplained blank area. The JavaScript D3 specialization builds on the same principles for richer scales, joins and interaction; it is a continuation, not a replacement for data validation.
chapters.anatomy: Use array.filter to derive records without mutating the source array. Create cells with createElement and textContent. Count the resulting rows and compare with the stated filter. For later D3 work, preserve stable record identities and separate data transformation from visual encoding. Never imply that a client-side filter is access control over confidential data already sent to the browser.

chapters.title: Browser trust boundaries: text, origins and policy
key_terms: Origin
The scheme, host and port of a URL; two URLs share an origin only when all three match.
Same-origin policy
The browser rule that stops a script from reading another origin's responses or documents by default.
Content Security Policy
A response header, CSP for short, that limits where scripts and other resources may load from, reducing the damage of injection.
Injection
Untrusted data being interpreted as markup, script or a command because it was inserted into the wrong context.
Sandbox
The `sandbox` attribute on an `iframe`, which removes abilities such as running scripts unless they are granted back explicitly.
chapters.mental:
An origin is generally a combination of scheme, host and port. The browser uses origins to separate access to data and documents. The same-origin policy is not a complete application security system; a server still needs authentication, authorization and deliberate cross-origin behavior. CORS is a protocol for relaxing some browser response-reading restrictions, not a mechanism that makes an unsafe endpoint safe.

Injection occurs when data is interpreted as code or structure in a context where it should remain data. textContent avoids HTML parsing for text, while building an href still requires a separate URL policy. Content Security Policy can reduce what a document may load or execute, but it is a defense layer rather than a replacement for correct output handling. The classroom preview is deliberately isolated and network restricted.
chapters.anatomy: Treat rendering contexts separately: HTML text, quoted HTML attribute, URL, JavaScript and CSS each have different rules. This reference renders an attack-shaped string only as text. No attack is performed against another site. A sandboxed iframe can have an opaque origin, so do not assume localStorage, cookies or a same-origin parent API exists inside the preview.

Validate the scheme before using a URL in navigation.

Different ports form different origins even when the host matches.

Render an angle-bracket string safely as visible text.
No extra element or event handler is created.
Assign the string with textContent and inspect the element tree.
