Build a small rendering demo that separates text handling from URL policy.
Plain text remains data and navigation candidates pass an explicit scheme decision.
Handle text and URLs in two separate functions with separate rules.
Text needs safe insertion, while URLs need an explicit allowlist of schemes before they become navigation targets.
Explain why CORS is not authorization.
Non-browser clients can still send requests, and the server must enforce permissions.
Ask what stops a command-line client from calling the same API.

Inspect the preview without relying on cookies or parent-window access.

Escaping stops data from being interpreted as code in one context, validation limits accepted values, CSP limits what the page may load or run, and sandboxing isolates a document's capabilities.
chapters.mistakes: Do not advertise a sanitizer based on replacing a few characters in every possible context. Avoid weakening the classroom sandbox to make a remote demo work. A policy failure is evidence about a restricted capability, not a reason to disable all protections.

chapters.title: Browser quality: tests, performance and independent review
key_terms: Acceptance test
A check that a user-visible requirement holds, written as steps plus an expected observation.
Rendering pipeline
The browser's work from style calculation through layout and paint to compositing that turns the DOM into pixels.
Performance measurement
Timing a realistic task, such as with `performance.now()`, several times with the inputs and conditions recorded.
Microbenchmark
Timing a tiny isolated operation, which explains that local task but says nothing about page load or production capacity.
chapters.mental:
Quality is a set of observable contracts. A structural test can check that a button has a label. An interaction test can check that it changes the intended value. A visual inspection can reveal clipping after resizing. An assistive-technology review can expose an announcement problem. No single kind of test proves all of these. Plan the evidence around the behavior you claim.

Performance also requires a defined workload and measurement boundary. Loading, parsing, scripting, layout, painting and network transfer contribute differently. A tiny function timer is not page-load performance. Warm caches, device speed, background activity and instrumentation affect measurements. Report the conditions and distributions instead of declaring an arbitrary universal millisecond target.
chapters.anatomy: Use explicit assertions that throw on failure rather than relying only on console.assert. Keep a deterministic fixture for logic tests and a separate manual checklist for keyboard, zoom, narrow width, print and reduced motion. Measure a bounded task with performance.now only when explaining that local task. Do not interpret a microbenchmark as a production capacity claim.
examples: Failure stops the claimed successful path.
A structural mismatch becomes an explicit failure.
The label states exactly what was timed.
The number describes one tiny local task, not total page performance.
tasks: Map a label, interaction and layout claim to different evidence.
Use structural checks, actual interaction and visual inspection respectively.
For each claim, ask whether it is about structure, behavior or appearance.
Structure can be checked in the DOM, behavior needs a real interaction and appearance needs visual inspection.
Turn one silent assumption into a throwing assertion.
A violated invariant produces a clear failure message.
Find an assumption the page relies on and throw a clear Error when it is false.
An explicit assertion turns a silent wrong state into a visible failure with a useful message.
Create a quality report for the portal from web-024.
The report records source revision, tested conditions, observations and remaining limitations.
Record the source revision, the conditions tested, what you observed and what remains untested.
A dated, scoped report lets someone else repeat the review and see its limits.
Diagnose a test that passes before an interaction later throws.
Inspect the settled state and errors after all representative actions.
Perform every representative action before reading the result.
A check that runs before the interaction misses errors that only happen after it.
Repeat the review after narrow resizing and a saved-page reload.
The interface remains usable and the learner distinguishes persisted source from transient preview state.
Resize the preview, reload the saved page and repeat the main tasks.
Reloading separates what was saved, the source, from transient preview state.
Explain what evidence would justify a production readiness claim.
It requires broader integration, security, accessibility, operational and workload-specific performance evidence than one local reference run.
List the kinds of evidence a production launch needs beyond one local run.
Production readiness needs integration, security, accessibility, operational and real-workload performance evidence that a single preview cannot supply.
chapters.mistakes: Avoid tests that merely search for a success string without exercising behavior. Do not erase a failure transcript when retrying. A successful browser run applies to that tested browser and source, not automatically to all devices.

reasoning.approach: Assign each claim a matching method: query the DOM for labels, press keys for interaction, and look at the rendered page for layout.
reasoning.pitfall: Using a DOM query to prove that a layout fits fails because the structure can be correct while elements overflow visually.
reasoning.verify: Your table pairs the label, interaction and layout claims with three different methods, and each row has its own recorded result and date.

reasoning.approach: Write `if (!condition) throw new Error('...')` with a message that names the expected and the actual value.
reasoning.pitfall: Using `console.assert` fails because it only logs the problem and lets the run end looking successful.
reasoning.verify: Breaking the condition makes the script stop with your message instead of reaching the final log line.

reasoning.approach: Record the source revision or file date, the browser and window size, and a line for each check with what happened.
reasoning.pitfall: Writing a report that says only all good fails because no reader can tell which conditions were checked or when.
reasoning.verify: Another person can repeat each check from your report alone and compare their results line by line.

reasoning.approach: Run every representative interaction first, then read the console and DOM in the settled state before declaring a result.
reasoning.pitfall: Asserting only on initial load fails because an error thrown after the first click never reaches the test.
reasoning.verify: After the full interaction sequence, the console shows no uncaught errors and the final state matches expectations.

reasoning.approach: Resize to the narrow preset, interact, save the source, reload, and compare which values persist and which reset.
reasoning.pitfall: Assuming a counter value survives reload fails because in-memory state is cleared and only saved source remains.
reasoning.verify: After reload the counter shows its starting value again, while your edited source changes are still present and the narrow layout still has no sideways scrolling.

reasoning.approach: List evidence types a production claim needs: integration tests, security review, accessibility audit, operations plan and load measurements.
reasoning.pitfall: Citing a fast `performance.now` timing fails because one tiny sort says nothing about real traffic, devices or data sizes.
reasoning.verify: Your answer names at least four evidence types, none of which this local reference run provides.

contrast.heading: console.assert as the only check
contrast.setup: Both snippets inspect the same broken page that has two `main` elements. Compare how the test run ends.
contrast.reading: When its condition is false, `console.assert` writes an Assertion failed message to the console and then lets execution continue, so All checks done still prints and anyone reading only the last line believes the page passed. The `throw` version stops at the first broken invariant, and the uncaught Error is reported as a failure with its message. A test runner that inspects exceptions or exit status can detect only the second form. Keep `console.assert` for quick local hints, not for quality evidence.

chapters.title: PHP begins: interpreter, CLI and server execution
key_terms: PHP interpreter
The program that reads a PHP script, compiles it to internal instructions and runs them.
CLI
The command-line interface, which runs a PHP script as a process and writes its output to standard output rather than an HTTP response.
Statement
One instruction ended by a semicolon, such as an assignment or an `echo`.
Server response
The status, headers and body a web server returns when PHP runs for an HTTP request instead of from the command line.
chapters.mental:
PHP is a programming language whose interpreter executes source instructions. In the classroom, a Linux CLI worker runs one file and captures its output. On a web server, a PHP runtime can instead receive request context and produce an HTTP response. These environments share language syntax but expose different inputs and lifecycle behavior. Printing a string that looks like HTML does not turn a CLI process into a web server.

PHP source begins with an opening tag, and statements commonly end with semicolons. Variables begin with a dollar sign. A comment explains source without executing it. Echo writes output; it does not return a value from a function or save data to a database. We start with literal strings and a tiny computed value so each step is visible.
chapters.anatomy: Use a pure PHP file beginning with `<?php`, followed by `declare(strict_types=1);` before other statements. Strict typing affects certain scalar type coercions at function call boundaries; it does not turn PHP into a statically typed language. Omit the closing tag in a pure PHP file to avoid accidental trailing output. Syntax errors occur before the intended program can run, while runtime errors occur during execution.
examples: A string literal becomes text in stdout.
One greeting line appears in the CLI output.
A variable makes the data's role explicit.
The dot operator concatenates the label and value.
tasks: Predict which characters in the greeting source appear in output.
The opening tag and echo keyword do not appear; the string content does.
Separate what the interpreter reads as instructions from what echo receives as a string.
The `<?php` tag and `echo` are PHP syntax, so only the string's characters, including the newline written as `\n`, reach the output.
Change the planned minutes while preserving the label.
Only the numeric portion changes.
Change only the value assigned to the variable.
The label is a separate string literal, so changing `$minutes` alters only the number that concatenation inserts.
Write a PHP program that prints a study topic and computed duration.
The program runs in the CLI worker and produces two clearly labeled values.
Store the topic and the minutes in variables, compute the duration, then echo two labeled lines.
Named values and one computation keep the program readable and let you verify the output by hand.
Diagnose a missing semicolon as a parse error.
The interpreter cannot execute the intended statement sequence until syntax is repaired.
Delete one semicolon, run the program and read the reported line number.
PHP parses the whole file before running it, so a syntax error stops execution and the reported line is often the one after the missing semicolon.
Print literal angle brackets and explain the output surface.
The CLI displays text; it does not automatically render a web page.
Echo a string that contains < and > and read the CLI output.
The CLI writes plain text to standard output, so angle brackets are printed as characters; no browser parses them as HTML.
Compare the CLI lifecycle with a server request lifecycle.
A CLI process receives its prepared inputs; a server integration supplies HTTP context and response handling.
List what a server provides to a request that a CLI run does not have.
A server integration supplies the request method, headers, cookies and a response channel for each request, while a CLI run receives only its own fixed inputs and exits.
chapters.mistakes: Do not paste PHP into an HTML-only preview expecting a server interpreter. A closing tag can introduce accidental whitespace output. Keep a syntax failure separate from a successful execution that produced the wrong value.

reasoning.approach: Separate the PHP syntax from the data: the tag and the `echo` keyword are instructions, while the quoted string is what gets written.
reasoning.pitfall: Expecting `<?php` to appear in the output fails because the interpreter consumes the opening tag and never prints it.
reasoning.verify: Running the file in the CLI worker prints Hello, classroom. followed by a single newline and nothing else.

reasoning.approach: Change only the value assigned to `$minutes` and leave the label string and the concatenation unchanged.
reasoning.pitfall: Editing the number inside the label string fails because the variable still holds 30, so the printed value disagrees with the plan.
reasoning.verify: After setting `$minutes = 45;`, the output reads Planned minutes: 45 with the label exactly as before.

reasoning.approach: Assign the topic and the session length to variables, compute the duration with an expression, and echo two labeled lines.
reasoning.pitfall: Printing the raw number without a label fails because a reader of the CLI output cannot tell which value is which.
reasoning.verify: The worker output shows two lines, each beginning with its label, and the computed value matches a hand calculation.

reasoning.approach: Read the line number in the parse error, look at the end of the previous statement, and add the missing semicolon.
reasoning.pitfall: Searching the output for a partial result fails because a parse error stops the file before any statement runs at all.
reasoning.verify: After adding the semicolon, the program runs and prints every line instead of a single parse error.

reasoning.approach: Echo a string such as `<strong>` and note that the CLI worker prints characters to a text stream rather than rendering markup.
reasoning.pitfall: Expecting bold text in the CLI output fails because no browser parses the string, so the tags appear as plain characters.
reasoning.verify: The worker output shows the literal text <strong> unchanged, with no change in font weight.

reasoning.approach: Describe where inputs come from in each case: prepared arguments for the CLI process, and request data plus headers for a server request.
reasoning.pitfall: Assuming `$_GET` is filled when running the CLI worker fails because no HTTP request exists, so those arrays stay empty.
reasoning.verify: Dumping `$_GET` in the CLI worker prints an empty array, while the program's prepared input values are present.

contrast.heading: a closing tag followed by blank lines
contrast.setup: This file ends with a closing tag, then two empty lines that are easy to miss in an editor.
contrast.code:
<?php
declare(strict_types=1);

echo "Hello, classroom.\n";
?>
contrast.reading: PHP swallows a single newline directly after `?>`, but every character after that is template text, so this CLI run prints the greeting followed by extra blank lines. In a web response the same stray output is sent before any later `header()` call, which then fails because headers are already sent. Deleting the closing tag removes the risk, because a pure PHP file then has no template area at the end. The fixed file prints exactly one greeting line in the CLI worker.

chapters.title: Values, types, strict comparisons and null
key_terms: Scalar type
One of PHP's single-value types, `int`, `float`, `string` and `bool`.
Strict comparison
The `===` operator, which is true only when both the value and the type match, unlike the converting `==`.
Null
The value that represents absence; a nullable type such as `?int` accepts an integer or null.
Null coalescing operator
The `??` operator, which returns its left side when that is set and not null, and its right side otherwise.
chapters.mental:
A value has a type that influences allowed operations and comparison behavior. PHP provides integers, floating-point numbers, strings, booleans, arrays, objects and null among its types. Null commonly represents absence, but its meaning belongs to the application's contract. Zero, an empty string and false are different values and should not be casually treated as interchangeable missing data.

Loose comparison can coerce values before comparison; strict comparison checks both type and value. The string '0' and integer 0 may look similar when printed but are different under strict equality. A form normally supplies strings, so validation and explicit conversion are necessary before treating them as trusted numeric data. Strict typing at function boundaries does not validate arbitrary request arrays.
chapters.anatomy: Use `===` and `!==` when type distinctions are part of the contract. `get_debug_type` helps inspect the type. The null-coalescing operator `??` supplies a default for an absent or null value, while `array_key_exists` can distinguish a present null entry from a missing key. Floating-point values approximate many decimal fractions, so financial examples later use integer minor units.
examples: The printed characters do not determine the comparison semantics.
The application decides whether null is meaningful.
The key exists, but the coalescing expression uses the fallback.
tasks: Predict strict equality for '0', 0 and false.
Each has a different type, so cross-type strict comparisons are false.
Write the type of each value before comparing any of them.
=== compares type and value, so a string, an integer and a boolean are never strictly equal to each other.
Add a typed diagnostic to a value before converting it.
The output identifies the actual type rather than relying on its printed appearance.
Print get_debug_type() or var_dump output next to the value.
A typed diagnostic shows whether '0' is a string or an integer, which echo alone hides.
Model an optional note without confusing missing, empty and null.
The program documents and checks the chosen interpretation of each state.
Decide what a missing key, an empty string and null each mean before writing code.
array_key_exists distinguishes a missing key from a key holding null, while ?? treats both the same, so the chosen meaning must be explicit.
Repair a loose comparison that accepts an unintended type.
Use strict comparison after deliberate validation and conversion.
Replace == with === after converting the value deliberately.
Loose comparison coerces types, so values such as '1' and true can compare equal unexpectedly; strict comparison after validation removes that surprise.
Test zero as a valid numeric boundary.
Zero is retained when the contract permits it, rather than discarded as generic falsy data.
Include 0 in your test inputs and check that it is kept.
0 is falsy, so a truthiness check such as `if ($minutes)` drops a valid zero; compare with null or use a range check instead.
Explain the limited scope of strict_types.
It affects relevant scalar call coercions; it does not replace runtime validation or static analysis.
Call a typed function with a numeric string with and without declare(strict_types=1).
strict_types controls scalar coercion for calls made from that file; it does not validate ranges, formats or array contents at runtime.
chapters.mistakes: Do not use empty() as a universal validation rule because it treats several distinct values as empty. Compare floating-point results with an appropriate tolerance when approximation is expected. A type declaration is not an input sanitizer.

reasoning.approach: Note the type of each value, string, int and bool, and recall that `===` returns false whenever the two types differ.
reasoning.pitfall: Using `==` and reporting true fails because loose comparison converts types first and hides the distinction the question asks about.
reasoning.verify: Running `var_export` on each strict pair prints false three times.

reasoning.approach: Print `get_debug_type($value)` before converting, so the output names the actual type such as string or int.
reasoning.pitfall: Printing the value with `echo` fails because '30' and 30 look identical in output while their types differ.
reasoning.verify: The diagnostic line reads string for the raw input and int after the deliberate conversion.

reasoning.approach: Use `array_key_exists` to detect a missing key, then check for null, then check for an empty string, each with a stated meaning.
reasoning.pitfall: Using `empty($record['note'])` fails because it treats a missing key, null, '' and '0' as the same state.
reasoning.verify: Four test records, missing, null, empty and a real note, each produce a different documented label.

reasoning.approach: Validate the input with a pattern or a filter, convert it explicitly with `(int)`, and then compare with `===`.
reasoning.pitfall: Adding a cast inside a loose comparison fails because the loose operator still accepts other spellings you did not intend.
reasoning.verify: The repaired check rejects '1e1' when only '10' is allowed and accepts the exact expected value.

reasoning.approach: Run the program with 0 as a valid entry and confirm that a strict null check, not truthiness, decides whether it is kept.
reasoning.pitfall: Writing `if ($minutes)` fails because 0 is falsy, so a legitimate zero entry is skipped as if it were missing.
reasoning.verify: The output lists the zero entry, and the total includes it as 0 rather than omitting the row.

reasoning.approach: State that `strict_types` changes how scalar arguments are coerced at function calls in this file, and nothing more.
reasoning.pitfall: Claiming strict mode validates form input fails because data from requests is still a string that needs explicit checks.
reasoning.verify: Passing '30' to an `int` parameter under strict mode throws a TypeError, while comparisons elsewhere are unaffected.

contrast.heading: loose equality between strings and other types
contrast.setup: Each comparison below prints true with `==`. Rewrite each with `===` and compare the results.
contrast.reading: Loose equality converts operands first. Two numeric strings are compared as numbers, so `'1e1'` and `'10'` are equal because both mean ten. The string `'0'` converts to false, and an empty string loosely equals null. With `===` all of these are false because the types or exact string contents differ, which is what the last line prints. If a role code or an identifier is checked with `==`, a different spelling can pass, so validation code in this course uses strict comparison after deliberate conversion.

chapters.title: Expressions, integer money and deliberate conversion
key_terms: Expression
Code that produces a value, such as `$a + 2` or a function call.
Operator precedence
The rules that decide which operator binds first, such as `*` before `+`; parentheses make the intended order explicit.
Integer minor units
Storing money as a whole number of the smallest unit, such as cents, to avoid floating-point rounding errors.
Integer range
The limits of PHP's `int` type; a result beyond `PHP_INT_MAX` becomes a float, so larger values need another representation.
chapters.mental:
An expression produces a value. Arithmetic operators combine numbers, concatenation joins strings, and logical operators combine conditions. Parentheses make intended grouping clear when an expression mixes operations. Do not assume that familiar-looking operators have the same precedence in every language or version. A readable intermediate variable is often safer than a dense one-line formula.

Many decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly by binary floating point. For a small money example, represent amounts as integer cents and define rounding when converting from external decimal text. This avoids accidentally treating a display string as a precise numeric representation. Integer arithmetic still has limits: values outside the supported range need a different numeric representation or library.
chapters.anatomy: Compute subtotal cents as unit cents times quantity, then add a fixed fee. Validate quantity before multiplication. Use intdiv for deliberate integer division and the remainder operator for the remaining cents. This lesson does not accept arbitrary decimal currency strings; that parser would need explicit scale, sign, range and rounding rules.
examples: The unit is encoded in the variable name.
The total is exactly 375 cents within the integer range.
Integer division and remainder produce two decimal digits.
tasks: Predict 125 cents times three units.
The result is 375 cents.
Multiply the integer cents first and convert to a display format only at the end.
125 × 3 is 375 cents; keeping integer minor units avoids binary floating-point rounding.
Add a fixed 50-cent fee with a named intermediate value.
The new total is 425 cents and the unit remains explicit.
Name the fee as its own variable before adding it.
A named intermediate keeps the unit visible: 375 + 50 = 425 cents.
Implement a bounded quantity calculation and cents formatter.
Valid quantities produce exact integer totals and two-digit fractional display.
Validate the quantity first, then use intdiv and % to split dollars and cents.
intdiv gives whole units and % gives the remainder, which str_pad formats as two digits.
Diagnose a concatenation expression that hides arithmetic grouping.
Use parentheses or intermediate variables to express the intended computation.
Add parentheses around the arithmetic inside the concatenation.
Since PHP 8, + and - bind tighter than ., but explicit parentheses or an intermediate variable still make the intended grouping obvious to readers.
Reject a negative quantity and test zero.
Invalid negative input is rejected; zero follows the declared contract.
Add a check that throws for negative quantities and run it with -1 and 0.
A negative quantity has no meaning for a purchase, while zero is a valid empty order unless the contract says otherwise.
Explain when integer cents are insufficient.
Different currency scales, huge ranges, exchange rates or fractional-unit pricing require an explicit broader numeric policy.
List cases where two decimal places or 64-bit integers are not enough.
Currencies with three decimal places, exchange rates and fractional unit prices need an explicit scale or a decimal library.
chapters.mistakes: Do not convert a formatted currency label back into a number by deleting random characters. Avoid claiming floating point is universally bad; it is appropriate for many approximate scientific calculations. Define the precision contract first.

reasoning.approach: Multiply the integer unit price in cents by the integer quantity, which keeps the whole calculation in exact integer arithmetic.
reasoning.pitfall: Computing 1.25 times 3 as floats and then multiplying by 100 fails because float rounding can produce a value just under 375.
reasoning.verify: `var_export($unitCents * $quantity)` prints 375 with no decimal point. Printing `get_debug_type` of the product shows int, confirming no float entered the calculation.

reasoning.approach: Store the fee in `$feeCents = 50`, add it to the subtotal in a separate named line, and keep every variable name ending in Cents.
reasoning.pitfall: Adding 0.5 for the fee fails because it mixes dollars and cents and turns the total into a float with the wrong scale.
reasoning.verify: The program prints 425 for the total and every intermediate value is an int in `get_debug_type`.

reasoning.approach: Validate the quantity as an integer within bounds, multiply in cents, then format with `intdiv`, `%` and `str_pad` to two digits.
reasoning.pitfall: Formatting with `$total / 100` fails because division produces a float and 305 cents may print as 3.05 or as 3.0499999.
reasoning.verify: Totals of 375, 305 and 5 cents format as 3.75, 3.05 and 0.05.

reasoning.approach: Wrap the arithmetic in parentheses or compute it into a named variable before concatenating it with the label text.
reasoning.pitfall: Relying on readers to know that `+` binds tighter than `.` in `'Total: ' . $a + $b` fails because the grouping is invisible and differed in PHP 7.
reasoning.verify: The repaired line prints Total: followed by the sum, and a reader can see the grouping without operator tables.

reasoning.approach: Check `$quantity < 0` before multiplying and throw a clear exception, while letting 0 produce a 0 cent subtotal.
reasoning.pitfall: Using `abs($quantity)` to fix negatives fails because a refund or a typo is silently turned into a valid purchase.
reasoning.verify: Quantity -1 raises the declared error and quantity 0 prints 0.00 as the subtotal. A quantity of 2 still prints 2.50 for a 125 cent unit price.

reasoning.approach: Name the cases integers cannot cover alone: three decimal currencies, exchange rates, very large totals and prices below one cent.
reasoning.pitfall: Assuming every currency uses two decimal places fails because some use zero or three, so a fixed 100 divisor is wrong.
reasoning.verify: Your answer lists at least one currency scale other than two and explains which extra rule it needs.

contrast.heading: money stored as floats
contrast.setup: This version represents prices in dollars as floats. Print the result two ways and compare with the integer version from worked example 1.
contrast.reading: Binary floating point cannot represent 0.1 or 0.2 exactly, so their sum is slightly larger than 0.3. `echo` rounds to the configured display precision and shows 0.3, which makes the value look correct. The strict comparison with 0.3 is false, and `var_export` prints the full value 0.30000000000000004. Across many line items these tiny differences can change a rounded total or make an equality check fail. The integer version stores 10 and 20 cents, adds them to exactly 30, and the comparison is true. That is why this lesson keeps every amount in integer cents and only formats a decimal label at output time.

chapters.title: Conditions, loops and bounded control flow
key_terms: Branch
A path chosen by a condition in `if`, `elseif` or `else`.
Guard clause
An early `return` or `throw` that handles an invalid or trivial case first, so the main path stays simple.
Match expression
A `match` that compares with strict identity, returns a value and throws `UnhandledMatchError` when no arm matches.
Loop termination
The guarantee that a loop eventually stops, usually because each iteration moves toward a fixed bound.
chapters.mental:
Control flow determines which statements execute and how often. A branch chooses among alternatives, while a loop repeats a body for a sequence or condition. A loop needs a termination argument: a bounded collection, an advancing counter or another condition that is guaranteed to change. The classroom enforces execution limits, but a good program should still have its own understandable bound.

Guard clauses reject invalid conditions before the main computation. They reduce nesting and make accepted input clearer. A match expression compares strictly and returns a value; it differs from a switch statement's traditional loose comparison behavior and fall-through possibilities. Use the construct whose semantics fit the task rather than choosing the shortest spelling.
chapters.anatomy: A foreach loop visits array values and can also expose keys. A for loop makes initialization, condition and update explicit. In a match expression, each arm maps a condition to a result, and a default arm handles other values when that is appropriate. Do not silently map invalid input to a valid default if the contract requires rejection.
examples: The loop visits a finite array once.
Strict matching preserves the distinction between labels.
tasks: Trace the accumulator after each iteration.
It progresses through 20, 50 and 65.
Write the total after each loop iteration in a table.
The accumulator adds each element in turn, so it holds 20, 50 and then 65.
Add a guard against negative durations.
Invalid values fail before they enter the total.
Check each value before adding it and throw for negatives.
Validating inside the loop stops one bad value from silently corrupting the total.
Build a bounded weekly-duration summary with a route label.
The total and label follow the declared cases and terminate predictably.
Use foreach over a fixed array for the total and match for the route label.
foreach always terminates over a finite array, and match maps each declared case to one label.
Diagnose a while loop whose condition never changes.
Identify the missing progress step and replace it with a bounded iteration where possible.
Find the variable in the loop condition and check whether the body changes it.
A loop whose condition never changes never ends; foreach or a counter with a fixed bound guarantees progress.
Test an empty collection.
The total is zero without a special invalid array access.
Run the summary with an empty array.
foreach over an empty array runs zero times, so the total keeps its initial value of 0.
Explain match versus switch for a typed mapping.
Match returns a value and compares strictly; switch has different comparison and fall-through rules.
Pass an integer to a match keyed by strings and compare with switch.
match compares with === and throws UnhandledMatchError for an unmatched value, while switch compares loosely and falls through without break.
chapters.mistakes: Do not rely on a worker timeout as the algorithm's termination strategy. Avoid changing the collection unexpectedly while iterating. A default arm should not conceal an unknown state that needs an error.

reasoning.approach: Write a row per iteration with the current value and the running total, adding each element to the previous total.
reasoning.pitfall: Writing only the final total fails because a wrong intermediate step, such as starting at 20 instead of 0, is then invisible.
reasoning.verify: Echoing `$total` inside the loop prints 20, 50 and 65 on three lines.

reasoning.approach: Inside the loop, check `$minutes < 0` before adding and throw an exception that names the offending value.
reasoning.pitfall: Using `continue` to skip negatives fails because the total then looks valid while silently hiding a data problem.
reasoning.verify: An input of [20, -5] stops with the error message, and no total is printed for it. An input of [20, 30] still prints 50, so the guard rejects only invalid values.

reasoning.approach: Sum validated durations with `foreach`, then map the level to a label with `match`, adding a default arm only if unknown levels are allowed.
reasoning.pitfall: Using `while (true)` with a manual break fails because a missing exit condition makes the worker run until its time limit.
reasoning.verify: The summary prints the expected total and label for each level, and an unknown level follows the declared rule.

reasoning.approach: Find the variable in the `while` condition and look for the statement that should change it on each pass.
reasoning.pitfall: Adding a counter that breaks after 1000 passes fails because it hides the missing update and returns a wrong partial result.
reasoning.verify: After adding the update, the loop runs exactly as many times as the input requires and then stops. Adding an echo of the loop variable shows it changing on every pass until the condition becomes false.

reasoning.approach: Run the summary with `[]` and confirm the loop body never executes while the total stays at its starting value of 0.
reasoning.pitfall: Reading `$durations[0]` before the loop fails because an empty array has no first element and PHP emits a warning.
reasoning.verify: The program prints a total of 0 for an empty list and emits no warnings.

reasoning.approach: Compare the two forms on '0' and on false: `match` uses identity and returns a value, while `switch` compares loosely and can fall through.
reasoning.pitfall: Treating them as interchangeable fails because `switch` matches '0' against `case false`, while `match` does not.
reasoning.verify: Running the contrast case prints switch: false branch and match: string arm. Removing the string arm makes the `match` call throw an UnhandledMatchError for '0'.

contrast.heading: switch versus match on a string zero
contrast.setup: Both blocks receive the string '0' from a form field. Trace which branch each one selects.
contrast.reading: `switch` compares with loose equality, and the string '0' loosely equals false, so it prints switch: false branch even though the value is a string. `match` uses strict identity, so the false arm does not match and the string arm does, printing match: string arm. If the string arm were removed, `match` would throw an `UnhandledMatchError` instead of quietly choosing a branch, which surfaces the unexpected value. That strictness is why worked example 2 uses `match` for a mapping where each input should land in one deliberate case. With `switch`, remember also that a missing `break` lets execution fall through into the next case.

chapters.title: Arrays, records, keys and transformations
key_terms: Ordered map
PHP's array type, which stores key and value pairs in insertion order with integer or string keys.
Record
An array with fixed string keys, such as a name and a score, used to describe one item.
Array filter
The `array_filter()` function, which keeps elements whose callback returns true and preserves their original keys.
Array values
The `array_values()` function, which renumbers keys from zero, often used after filtering to restore a list.
Mapping
Transforming every element with a callback, such as with `array_map()`, to produce a new array of results.
chapters.mental:
PHP's array is an ordered map: it associates keys with values and preserves an iteration order. It can represent a list or a keyed record, but these are different data contracts. A list of study rows should not accidentally become an object-shaped JSON value because filtered numeric keys were left nonconsecutive. Key coercion can also matter, so avoid treating arbitrary external strings as interchangeable with integer indices.

Transformations are easier to reason about when they do not mutate the original data unexpectedly. Map computes a derived value for each record; filter keeps records satisfying a predicate. Validate expected fields before arithmetic. A missing key is different from a known null field and should be handled according to the record contract.
chapters.anatomy: Use explicit string keys for records, such as subject and minutes. `array_filter` preserves keys, so `array_values` is useful when the intended result is a fresh list. `array_map` applies a function to values. PHP 8.4 adds `array_find`, which returns the first matching value or null, and `array_any` and `array_all`, which answer yes-or-no questions without building an intermediate array. A foreach by reference can leave a lingering reference to the last item; avoid it unless mutation is necessary and understood.
examples: Keys name the meaning of each value.
Reindexing preserves the intended list shape.
The result uses consecutive list indices.
tasks: Explain how a list differs from a keyed record.
A list models ordered values; a record's named keys identify fields.
Compare how you refer to an item: by position or by name.
A list uses consecutive integer positions, while a record's string keys name its fields.
Add a second validated study row.
Every row has the declared subject and integer-minutes fields.
Copy the first row's keys exactly and check the minutes type.
Records with the same keys and types can be processed by one function without special cases.
Filter and summarize study records without changing the originals.
The derived list contains only qualifying rows and retains consecutive indices.
Filter into a new variable and leave the original array untouched.
array_filter returns a new array, and array_values renumbers it into a list.
Diagnose JSON output changing from an array to an object shape.
Inspect numeric key gaps after filtering and reindex when the contract is a list.
Print the array keys after filtering.
array_filter preserves keys, so gaps such as 0 and 2 make json_encode produce an object instead of a list.
Test an empty result and a missing required field.
Empty lists are valid where declared; malformed records are rejected explicitly.
Filter with a threshold above every value and also pass a record missing minutes.
An empty list is a valid result, while a malformed record must be rejected before it is used.
Explain the risk of a lingering foreach reference.
A reference variable can still alias the last element and cause later assignments to mutate it.
Use foreach with `&$item` and then reuse `$item` in a second loop.
After a by-reference loop, `$item` still points at the last element, so a later assignment overwrites it; `unset($item)` breaks the reference.
chapters.mistakes: Do not assume every array is a list. Avoid weakly typed mixed records whose missing fields become warnings during rendering. Keep mutation deliberate and test the original data after transformations.

reasoning.approach: Describe a list as positions 0, 1, 2 holding values of one kind, and a record as named keys each holding a different field.
reasoning.pitfall: Storing a record as `['CSS', 55]` fails because code must remember that position 1 means minutes, which breaks when fields are added.
reasoning.verify: Accessing `$row['minutes']` on the keyed record prints 55 and reads clearly in the code.

reasoning.approach: Append a second array with the same `subject` and `minutes` keys, and check that minutes is an int with `is_int`.
reasoning.pitfall: Spelling the key as `minute` in the new row fails because later code reads `minutes` and gets a missing key warning.
reasoning.verify: A loop over both rows prints each subject and minutes with no warnings. `array_column($rows, 'minutes')` returns two integers, one per row.

reasoning.approach: Use `array_filter` with a typed arrow function, wrap it in `array_values`, then sum with `array_sum(array_column($visible, 'minutes'))`.
reasoning.pitfall: Modifying `$rows` inside a `foreach` by reference fails because the original data changes and a later filter sees altered values.
reasoning.verify: After the summary, dumping `$rows` shows the original records unchanged, and the derived list has keys 0 upward.

reasoning.approach: Encode the filtered array, notice an object with numeric keys, and add `array_values` before encoding to restore a list.
reasoning.pitfall: Passing `JSON_FORCE_OBJECT` or changing the client fails because the real problem is the key gap in the PHP array.
reasoning.verify: `json_encode` after reindexing prints a value that starts with `[` instead of `{`. A JavaScript client can then call `.map` on the parsed value without a TypeError.

reasoning.approach: Run the filter with a threshold no row meets, and run validation on a row lacking `minutes`, recording both outcomes.
reasoning.pitfall: Using `$row['minutes'] ?? 0` for missing fields fails because a broken record silently becomes a valid zero minute session.
reasoning.verify: The empty filter encodes as [] and the malformed row raises the declared validation error.

reasoning.approach: Call `unset($row)` after any `foreach ($rows as &$row)` loop so the reference no longer points at the last element.
reasoning.pitfall: Reusing `$row` in a second plain `foreach` fails because each assignment then overwrites the last element of the array.
reasoning.verify: Without `unset`, the last record ends up duplicated; with `unset`, all records keep their original values.

contrast.heading: filtered keys leaking into JSON
contrast.setup: The filter is correct, but the result is encoded directly. Compare the JSON with and without reindexing.
contrast.reading: `array_filter` keeps the original keys, so `$kept` holds keys 1 and 2. Because the keys no longer start at 0 and run consecutively, `json_encode` cannot represent the array as a list and produces the object {"1":50,"2":45}. A JavaScript client that calls `.map` on that value then fails, since objects have no `map` method. After `array_values` the keys are 0 and 1 and the output is the list [50,45]. Filtering that keeps the first element would hide this bug, so test with data where an early item is removed.

chapters.title: Functions, contracts, closures and reusable logic
key_terms: Function contract
The parameter types, return type and documented behavior that a caller is allowed to rely on.
Return type
The declared type after a function's parameter list, which PHP checks when the function returns.
Closure
An anonymous function object that captures outer variables only through `use`, by value unless marked with `&`.
Arrow function
A short closure such as `fn($x) => $x * 2` that holds one expression and captures outer variables by value automatically.
Pure function
A function whose result depends only on its inputs and that has no side effects such as output or file writes.
chapters.mental:
A function gives a named operation explicit inputs and an output. A useful contract states accepted values, returned meaning and failure behavior. Type declarations communicate and enforce part of that contract at runtime, but a positive duration requirement needs an explicit value check in addition to an int type. Small pure functions are easy to test because their result depends on inputs rather than hidden global state.

A closure is a function value that can be passed to another function. Arrow functions capture variables from their surrounding scope by value automatically, while ordinary anonymous functions use an explicit use clause for capture. Avoid hidden mutable dependencies when a simple parameter would make the relationship clearer.
chapters.anatomy: Separate formatting from calculation so each can be tested independently. Return values are not the same as echo output. A function that echoes a result may be difficult to compose, while a function that returns a value lets a caller choose how to display it. Use exceptions for invalid inputs when the contract treats them as errors, and document predictable alternate results when absence is normal.
examples: The range check complements the type declaration.
A valid integer produces a doubled integer; a negative value fails.
The operation is passed as data to a transformation.
tasks: Explain the difference between returning and echoing a value.
Returning supplies data to the caller; echo writes output as a side effect.
Ask what the caller can do with the result in each case.
return hands a value back for further computation, while echo only writes output, which callers and tests cannot reuse.
Add a value-range guard to a typed function.
The function rejects invalid integers even though they satisfy the declared type.
Add a check that throws for negative minutes even though the type is int.
A type declaration accepts every int, so range rules need explicit checks.
Build reusable duration calculation and display functions.
Calculations can be tested without capturing output, then formatted at the boundary.
Keep the calculation pure and do the formatting in a separate function.
Pure functions can be tested by comparing return values, and formatting happens once at the output boundary.
Diagnose a result depending on an undocumented global.
Pass the dependency explicitly or isolate the stateful boundary.
Find every value the function reads that is not a parameter.
Hidden globals make results depend on outside state; passing values explicitly makes the function predictable.
Test zero, a normal value and a negative input.
Each follows the stated contract and the failure is intentional.
Call the function with 0, 30 and -1 and record each outcome.
Zero and a normal value follow the contract, and -1 must raise the declared exception.
Explain when a closure improves a transformation.
A short callback can express a local operation while keeping its inputs and captured context clear.
Write the transformation once with a named function and once with fn.
An arrow function suits a short, local operation and captures outer variables by value automatically.
chapters.mistakes: Do not hide output, database access and validation inside one large function merely to reduce file count. A type declaration cannot enforce every domain rule. Keep function names aligned with the actual responsibility.

reasoning.approach: Ask where the value ends up: `return` hands it to the calling expression, while `echo` writes to output and the caller receives nothing.
reasoning.pitfall: Saying the echoed text can be stored in a variable fails because the function returns null and the text has already been printed.
reasoning.verify: `var_dump(label(30))` for the echo version shows the text and then NULL, not the string.

reasoning.approach: Keep the `int` parameter type and add `if ($minutes < 0) throw new InvalidArgumentException(...)` before the calculation.
reasoning.pitfall: Relying on the `int` type alone fails because -5 is a valid integer and passes the type check.
reasoning.verify: Calling the function with -5 raises the exception, while 0 and 45 return results. The exception message names the rejected value, so the caller can show a precise correction.

reasoning.approach: Write `totalMinutes(array $sessions): int` for arithmetic and `formatMinutes(int $minutes): string` for display, and call echo only in the main script.
reasoning.pitfall: Putting `echo` inside `totalMinutes` fails because tests then need output capture and cannot simply compare returned integers.
reasoning.verify: A test compares `totalMinutes([20, 30])` with 50, and only the final script line prints anything.

reasoning.approach: Search the function body for `global` or `$GLOBALS`, then add that dependency as a parameter and pass it from the caller.
reasoning.pitfall: Setting the global before every call fails because a forgotten setup step silently changes results in unrelated code.
reasoning.verify: The function now gives the same result for the same arguments, whatever global variables exist. Running the function twice with different global values set no longer changes its output.

reasoning.approach: Call the function with 0, 45 and -1 in sequence, catching the expected exception only for the negative case.
reasoning.pitfall: Testing only 45 fails because the boundary at 0 and the error path are where contracts usually break.
reasoning.verify: The outputs are 0, 90 and one InvalidArgumentException message, matching the documented contract.

reasoning.approach: Use a short arrow function when the operation is local to one `array_map` call and reads naturally inline.
reasoning.pitfall: Writing a long closure that captures many outer variables fails because its real inputs are hidden and hard to test.
reasoning.verify: The arrow function `fn(int $value): int => $value * 2` maps [10, 20] to [20, 40]. The original input array still holds [10, 20] after the call, because `array_map` returns a new array.

contrast.heading: a formatter that echoes instead of returning
contrast.setup: The caller wants to build one sentence from the formatted duration. Trace the output order and the value of `$text`.
contrast.reading: PHP must evaluate `label(30)` before it can finish the concatenation, so 30 minutes is printed at that moment, before anything else. The function is declared `void`, so it returns null, and concatenating null adds nothing. `$text` becomes Total: and the program prints that on the next line. The output therefore shows the duration and the label separated and in the wrong order. Changing the return type to `string` and returning the text lets the caller decide where it goes.

chapters.title: Strings, UTF-8, bytes and contextual encoding
key_terms: UTF-8
An encoding that stores each Unicode code point in one to four bytes, with ASCII characters taking one byte.
Byte length
The count `strlen()` returns, which is the number of bytes, not the number of visible characters, for non-ASCII text.
Code point
One Unicode value, counted by `mb_strlen()` when the encoding is UTF-8.
Grapheme
What a reader perceives as one character, which can combine several code points, such as a letter with an accent mark.
chapters.mental:
A PHP string is a sequence of bytes. UTF-8 is an encoding that represents characters using one or more bytes, so strlen counts bytes rather than user-perceived characters. A visible character can also consist of multiple code points, such as a letter with a combining mark. Code-point count and grapheme count are therefore different concepts. Choose the measure that matches the product requirement.

This worker does not assume every optional internationalization extension. The examples use valid UTF-8 and demonstrate byte-level behavior plus a Unicode-aware regular expression. Production text normalization, locale-aware sorting and grapheme handling need deliberate library and extension choices. Do not truncate arbitrary UTF-8 bytes and then assume the result remains valid text.
chapters.anatomy: Use explicit UTF-8 when escaping HTML output. JSON requires valid Unicode data and can fail on invalid UTF-8. A Unicode regular expression with the u modifier interprets the pattern as UTF-8, but it is not a universal grapheme library. The mbstring functions count and cut by code point instead of byte: `mb_strlen('café')` is 4 while `strlen('café')` is 5, and `mb_strcut` truncates to a byte budget without splitting a character. PHP 8.4 adds `mb_trim`, `mb_ltrim` and `mb_rtrim` for Unicode whitespace. A code point is still not always one visible character, because an accent can be a separate combining code point. Keep validation, normalization and output encoding separate because they solve different problems.
examples: The byte length is 2 for this UTF-8 source character.
The encoder validates its input representation.
The result is valid JSON that preserves the readable Unicode label.
tasks: Predict the UTF-8 byte length of é.
It occupies two bytes in the supplied source encoding.
Count bytes, not letters: look at how UTF-8 encodes é.
é is U+00E9, which UTF-8 stores as two bytes, so strlen returns 2.
Encode a Unicode label as JSON with explicit error handling.
The output is valid JSON or a visible encoding exception.
Pass JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR so invalid data raises an exception.
Without the flag json_encode returns false on invalid UTF-8; with it, the failure is visible.
Build a text inspection report that labels bytes honestly.
The program does not present strlen as a count of user-perceived characters.
Report strlen as bytes and mb_strlen as code points, side by side.
Labeling each count prevents a byte count from being presented as characters.
Diagnose a truncated string that splits a multibyte sequence.
Byte slicing can create invalid UTF-8; use a suitable text-aware operation for the intended unit.
Cut the string with substr at a byte position inside é, then try mb_strcut.
substr can split a multibyte sequence and produce invalid UTF-8, while mb_strcut moves the cut back to a character boundary.
Compare a plain ASCII label and a Unicode label.
The byte counts differ from intuitive character counts when multibyte data appears.
Print strlen and mb_strlen for an ASCII label and for café.
ASCII characters use one byte each, so the counts match; café differs because é uses two bytes.
Explain validation, normalization and output escaping separately.
Validation checks a contract, normalization chooses an equivalent representation, and escaping protects a destination context.
Name the question each step answers.
Validation asks whether the value is allowed, normalization chooses one representation of equivalent text, and escaping makes the value safe for a specific output context.
chapters.mistakes: Do not promise that a regex character count equals a user's perceived character count. Avoid silently replacing invalid data without a declared policy. Text encoding matters before both rendering and storage.

reasoning.approach: Recall that é is encoded in UTF-8 as two bytes, so `strlen`, which counts bytes, returns 2 for that one visible character.
reasoning.pitfall: Answering 1 fails because `strlen` does not count characters, and using that number for limits truncates the text wrongly.
reasoning.verify: `strlen('é')` prints 2 while `mb_strlen('é', 'UTF-8')` prints 1.

reasoning.approach: Call `json_encode` with `JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR | JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE` inside a `try` and catch `JsonException` to report a failure.
reasoning.pitfall: Checking only for a false return without the flag fails because callers often concatenate false and print an empty string.
reasoning.verify: The output shows {"label":"café"} with readable é, and invalid input prints the caught exception.

reasoning.approach: Print byte length with `strlen`, code point length with `mb_strlen`, and label each number with its unit in the report.
reasoning.pitfall: Labeling the `strlen` result as characters fails because accented or emoji labels then report inflated counts.
reasoning.verify: For 'café' the report shows 5 bytes and 4 code points on separate labeled lines.

reasoning.approach: Replace `substr` with `mb_substr` for character limits, or with `mb_strcut` when the limit is a byte budget.
reasoning.pitfall: Trimming the broken byte with `rtrim` fails because it removes whitespace characters, not partial multibyte sequences.
reasoning.verify: The truncated label encodes as JSON without an exception and displays complete characters. `mb_check_encoding($short, 'UTF-8')` returns true for the repaired value and false for the byte slice.

reasoning.approach: Print `strlen` and `mb_strlen` for 'cafe' and 'café' side by side and compare both rows.
reasoning.pitfall: Testing only ASCII labels fails because byte and character counts agree there and hide the multibyte problem.
reasoning.verify: The ASCII row shows 4 and 4, while the accented row shows 5 and 4. Adding an emoji label shows an even larger gap, with 4 bytes for that single code point.

reasoning.approach: Assign each step its own purpose: validate that input meets the contract, normalize to one representation, and escape at output for its destination.
reasoning.pitfall: Running `htmlspecialchars` on input before storing it fails because the stored text is then wrong for JSON, SQL and plain text.
reasoning.verify: Your answer names one concrete function or check for each of the three steps and the stage where it runs.

contrast.heading: byte slicing a multibyte label
contrast.setup: Both lines try to keep the first four characters of a short label, then encode it as JSON.
contrast.reading: In UTF-8 'café' is five bytes because é uses two. `substr` counts bytes, so `$bytes` keeps c, a, f and only the first byte of é, which is not valid UTF-8. `mb_substr` counts code points and keeps the full word. The first `json_encode` prints the label normally. The second throws a `JsonException` for malformed UTF-8 because JSON requires valid Unicode. Without the throw flag, it would return false instead, which is easy to miss.

chapters.title: Structured data, streams and bounded file handling
key_terms: JSON decoding
Turning JSON text into PHP values with `json_decode()`, ideally with `JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR` so invalid input raises an exception.
Stream
PHP's abstraction for reading or writing sequential data, such as a file or memory, through a handle.
Resource
A special PHP value holding an open handle, such as a stream from `fopen()`, until it is closed.
Bounded input
Reading at most a fixed number of bytes or records, so oversized input cannot exhaust memory or time.
chapters.mental:
JSON is a data format, not a PHP object model or a validation system. Decoding can produce syntactically valid data with the wrong fields, wrong types or an unexpectedly deep structure. Treat parsing and contract validation as separate steps. The examples use tiny inline JSON and a temporary stream so no host path or persistent file is required.

A stream represents a readable or writable sequence of bytes. File operations can fail, return partial results or expose sensitive data if paths are chosen carelessly. In an application, accept an identifier and map it to an owned location instead of accepting an arbitrary user-supplied filesystem path. Bound size before reading untrusted content into memory, and close resources when finished.
chapters.anatomy: Use JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR so invalid JSON becomes an exception instead of an ambiguous null result. Pass true when an associative-array representation is intended, then validate each required field. `php://temp` provides a temporary stream suitable for this local demonstration. Check resource creation and write results, rewind before reading, and close in a finally block.
examples: Syntactic JSON validity is only the first step.

$data = json_decode('{"minutes":30}', true, 32, JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
if (!is_int($data['minutes'] ?? null)) throw new InvalidArgumentException('Expected integer minutes');
The record is accepted only after the field contract passes.
The resource belongs to this process.
tasks: Explain why valid JSON can still be invalid application input.
It may contain the wrong structure, types, ranges or required fields.
Decode a JSON document with the right syntax but the wrong field type.
json_decode only checks syntax, so types, ranges and required fields still need validation.
Add a bounded decoding depth and explicit parse errors.
Malformed or too-deep input produces an intentional failure.
Pass a depth limit and JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR to json_decode.
The depth limit bounds nesting, and the flag turns malformed input into a JsonException.
Parse a small study record and round-trip it through a temporary stream.
The field contract passes and the returned bytes match the encoded value.
Validate the decoded record, write it to php://temp, rewind, then read it back.
A temporary stream behaves like a file in memory, so the round trip shows that the written bytes equal the encoded value.
Diagnose an empty read caused by the stream cursor position.
Rewind before reading from the beginning.
Print `ftell($stream)` before reading.
After writing, the cursor sits at the end of the stream, so a read returns nothing until rewind moves it back.
Reject an unexpected field type and an oversized input string.
The program checks both byte budget and data contract before use.
Check strlen of the raw input before decoding and is_int on the field after decoding.
A byte budget limits work before parsing, and the field check rejects data that parses but breaks the contract.
Explain why user-controlled paths need an ownership policy.
A path can escape the intended data area or expose unrelated files; identifiers should map through a reviewed boundary.
Ask where ../../etc/passwd would lead if it reached a file function.
Paths from users can traverse outside the data area, so the program should map identifiers to files it owns.
chapters.mistakes: Do not disable warnings to hide failed I/O. A file existing does not prove that its content matches the schema. The lesson's temporary stream does not establish durable persistence across worker runs.

reasoning.approach: Separate syntax from meaning: decoding proves the text is JSON, while field checks prove it has the required keys, types and ranges.
reasoning.pitfall: Accepting any successfully decoded value fails because {"minutes":"thirty"} is valid JSON with the wrong field type.
reasoning.verify: That input decodes without error but is rejected by the `is_int` field check with a clear message. A record with `minutes` set to 30 passes the same check and continues to the next step.

reasoning.approach: Pass a depth of 32 and `JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR`, and catch `JsonException` where the input arrives.
reasoning.pitfall: Using the default depth with no flag fails because malformed input returns null, which looks the same as valid null.
reasoning.verify: Malformed text and an input nested deeper than the limit both reach the catch block with messages.

reasoning.approach: Decode, validate the record, encode it again, write it to `php://temp`, rewind, read it back and compare the strings.
reasoning.pitfall: Reading immediately after `fwrite` fails because the stream cursor sits at the end, so the read returns an empty string.
reasoning.verify: The value read after `rewind` is identical to the encoded string, and the field contract still passes.

reasoning.approach: Check where the cursor is with `ftell` after writing, then call `rewind` before reading from the start.
reasoning.pitfall: Reopening `php://temp` to read fails because each open creates a new empty stream, not the one you wrote.
reasoning.verify: `ftell` reports 5 after writing notes and 0 after `rewind`, and the read returns notes.

reasoning.approach: Check `strlen($input)` against a byte limit before decoding, then check the decoded field type with `is_int`.
reasoning.pitfall: Decoding first and measuring later fails because the oversized input has already used memory and processing time.
reasoning.verify: An input over the limit is rejected before `json_decode` runs, and a string `minutes` value is rejected after.

reasoning.approach: Map a short identifier through a reviewed allowlist to a file inside one data directory, never using the raw input as a path.
reasoning.pitfall: Joining user text onto a base directory fails because ../ segments can reach files outside the intended folder.
reasoning.verify: An identifier of ../secrets is rejected, while a listed identifier resolves to a file inside the data directory. Logging the resolved path with `realpath` shows it still begins with the data directory.

contrast.heading: json_decode without error reporting
contrast.setup: Two inputs reach the decoder: a truncated object and the literal JSON value null. Compare default mode with the throwing mode.
contrast.reading: In default mode both calls return NULL. The first input is malformed, while the second is valid JSON whose value really is null, and the return value cannot tell them apart. Code that continues with `$data['minutes'] ?? 0` would treat a broken upload as a zero minute record. With `JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR` the truncated input raises a `JsonException` and the catch block prints a rejection, while valid null still returns null for the field checks to reject. That separation is why worked example 1 parses with the flag before validating fields.

chapters.title: Exceptions, errors and useful failure boundaries
key_terms: Exception
An object thrown to signal an error, which unwinds the call stack until a matching `catch` handles it.
Throwable
The interface implemented by both `Exception` and `Error`, so catching it handles any thrown object.
Finally block
Code after `try` and `catch` that runs whether or not an exception was thrown, used for cleanup.
Error boundary
The one place, usually near the entry point, that catches unexpected failures, records them and returns a safe message.
chapters.mental:
An exception interrupts the ordinary flow and can be handled by a matching catch block. It is useful when a function cannot fulfill its contract. A catch block should either recover meaningfully, translate the error into an appropriate boundary response or rethrow it. Catching every failure and returning a normal-looking value can corrupt downstream reasoning.

PHP has different error categories, and not every warning automatically becomes an exception. Runtime configuration and library behavior matter. A production error boundary should avoid exposing stack traces, secrets or internal paths to visitors while retaining an appropriate diagnostic record for maintainers. The local classroom output is a teaching surface, not a production logging policy.
chapters.anatomy: Catch specific exceptions near an operation when a specific recovery exists. Use finally for cleanup that should happen whether the operation succeeds or fails. Keep validation errors distinct from unexpected internal failures. An invalid user field can produce a clear correction; an unavailable database may require a generic retry message and internal diagnosis.
examples: The caller can distinguish invalid input from a normal result.
Zero and negative values raise a declared exception.
Finally expresses ownership of a cleanup step.
The useful error is shown and the final step still runs.
tasks: Trace the statements executed after requirePositive(0).
The function throws, the matching catch runs and finally executes.
Follow the throw into the matching catch, then into finally.
requirePositive(0) throws before returning, the InvalidArgumentException catch runs, and finally always executes.
Add a specific catch around a recoverable validation error.
The caller presents a correction without hiding unrelated failures.
Catch only InvalidArgumentException around the call.
A narrow catch handles the expected validation error and lets unrelated errors surface.
Build a failure-aware parser with explicit success and error paths.
Valid data returns a result; invalid data produces a clear classified failure.
Return a result for valid data and throw a named exception for each kind of invalid data.
Distinct exception types let callers react to each failure and keep successful results clearly separate.
Diagnose a catch-all that returns zero for every failure.
A fabricated normal value hides the difference between valid zero and broken processing.
Find the catch block that returns 0 and ask how a caller tells it apart from a real zero.
Returning a normal-looking value on failure hides errors and corrupts later results.
Test cleanup after both success and exception.
Owned resources are released in either path.
Run the code once with valid input and once with invalid input, logging inside finally.
finally runs on both paths, so resources released there are always released.
Explain the difference between learner diagnostics and public production errors.
Detailed local diagnostics support learning, while public responses should avoid sensitive internal detail.
Compare the detail you need while learning with what an outside user should see.
Detailed diagnostics help locally, but public errors should give a safe message without stack traces, paths or secrets.
chapters.mistakes: Do not catch Throwable merely to print success. Avoid including secrets in exception messages. A handler that returns a valid-looking fallback must have a genuine domain reason and an observable warning where appropriate.

reasoning.approach: Follow control flow: the `throw` skips the `return`, PHP finds the matching catch, runs it, and then runs `finally` either way.
reasoning.pitfall: Expecting the line after the call inside `try` to run fails because a throw exits the `try` block immediately.
reasoning.verify: The output shows the error message followed by Attempt finished, and no result line. Changing the argument to 5 prints the result, skips the catch block and still prints Attempt finished.

reasoning.approach: Catch `InvalidArgumentException` only, show its message to the user, and let other exception types continue upward.
reasoning.pitfall: Catching `Exception` here fails because a database or file error would then be shown as if it were a typing mistake.
reasoning.verify: Invalid input prints the correction message, while a forced `RuntimeException` still stops the program.

reasoning.approach: Return either the parsed value or an error result with a message, and print each case on a separate labeled line.
reasoning.pitfall: Returning null for every failure fails because the caller cannot tell an empty input from an out of range number.
reasoning.verify: Inputs 30, '' and 500 produce a value, an empty input message and a range message respectively. Each failure line names the field and the rule it broke, so the reader can correct the input directly.

reasoning.approach: Replace `catch (Throwable)` with a specific catch and return a failure result instead of a valid looking number.
reasoning.pitfall: Logging the error but still returning 0 fails because totals stay wrong even though a log line exists.
reasoning.verify: With the repair, minutesOrZero('abc') no longer prints 0, and '0' still does. A deliberate TypeError inside `parseMinutes` now stops the run with a stack trace instead of becoming 0.

reasoning.approach: Open a resource in `try`, release it in `finally`, and run the code once with valid input and once with input that throws.
reasoning.pitfall: Putting cleanup after the `try` block fails because an exception skips that line, so the resource stays open.
reasoning.verify: A message printed in `finally` appears in both runs, once after the result and once after the error.

reasoning.approach: Keep full messages and stack traces in local CLI output or server logs, and show public users only a short generic reference.
reasoning.pitfall: Printing database credentials or file paths to the public page fails because attackers learn the internal layout.
reasoning.verify: The public error text contains no path, query or secret, while the local log entry has the details. Comparing the two messages side by side shows that only the log entry contains the exception class and line number.

contrast.heading: a catch-all that invents a zero
contrast.setup: This wrapper was added so the summary page never shows an error. Feed it a valid 0, the text abc and a parser bug.
contrast.reading: Both calls print 0. The first is a real value, the second is a validation failure, and a typo or a TypeError inside `parseMinutes` would also print 0. Because `Throwable` catches errors as well as exceptions, even a programming mistake becomes a normal looking duration, and totals quietly undercount. Catching `InvalidArgumentException` only, and returning a result that carries the error message, keeps 0 meaningful and lets unexpected errors still stop the run where they can be diagnosed.

chapters.title: Objects, constructors and immutable value boundaries
key_terms: Class
A definition of properties and methods; each object created from it with `new` is an instance.
Constructor
The `__construct()` method that runs when an object is created and should leave it in a valid state.
Invariant
A condition that must hold for every valid object, checked by the constructor and preserved by every method.
Readonly property
A property that can be assigned only once, during initialization inside the class, and never modified afterward.
chapters.mental:
A class defines a kind of object, and an object combines state with behavior. Use an object when it makes a domain boundary clearer, not merely because the program has grown. A constructor establishes the initial state. An invariant is a condition that should remain true throughout the object's useful lifetime, such as a nonempty topic and nonnegative duration.

Publicly mutable properties can let callers bypass a carefully checked constructor. A small immutable value object can preserve its contract by validating once and exposing readonly data. Readonly does not make every nested object deeply immutable, and it does not replace validation. Understand the specific language guarantee rather than treating the keyword as a complete architecture.
chapters.anatomy: Constructor property promotion can declare and initialize properties directly in the parameter list. Use explicit types and meaningful names. A method can derive a display label from the stored values without changing them. PHP 8.4 also offers asymmetric visibility, such as `public private(set) int $minutes`, for a property that anyone may read but only the class may change, and property hooks, which run code in a property's `get` or `set` operation. Use them when an object genuinely changes; a value object that never changes is still clearest with `readonly`. Prefer composition of small responsibilities over a deep inheritance hierarchy built before requirements are known.
examples: Construction is the point where the invariant is established.
Every successfully created Duration has nonnegative minutes.
The method computes from the object's state.
The value is readable without exposing a mutation operation.
tasks: Name the invariant enforced by the constructor.
A successfully constructed duration cannot begin with negative minutes.
Read the constructor's checks and state what they guarantee about every object.
Because the constructor throws for negative minutes and the property is readonly, every Duration object has nonnegative minutes for its whole life.
Add a method that formats the duration.
Formatting derives from state without changing it.
Add a method that returns a string built from the properties without assigning to them.
A method that only reads state keeps the object immutable and the formatting reusable.
Build a validated study-session value object.
Its topic and duration satisfy explicit constructor checks and remain readonly.
Validate topic and minutes in the constructor and declare both properties readonly.
Constructor validation plus readonly properties mean invalid sessions cannot be created or changed later.
Diagnose a setter that allows invalid state after construction.
Every mutation boundary must preserve the invariant, or mutation should be removed.
Find every place that can assign to the property after construction.
A setter without the constructor's checks lets invalid state in later, so it must validate the same rule or be removed.
Test an empty topic and zero duration.
The topic is rejected while zero follows the declared nonnegative policy.
Construct one object with an empty topic and one with zero minutes.
The empty topic violates the rule and throws, while zero minutes satisfies the nonnegative rule.
Explain shallow readonly versus deep immutability.
A readonly property cannot be reassigned, but referenced mutable objects can have their own changing state.
Make a readonly property hold an object and change that object's internals.
readonly prevents reassigning the property but not mutating the object it refers to, so deep immutability needs immutable members too.
chapters.mistakes: Do not build an inheritance tree for every noun. A readonly array cannot be changed through that property, but a readonly property referring to an object does not freeze that object's internals. Keep the claimed guarantee precise.

reasoning.approach: Read the constructor check and state its guarantee: any `Duration` that exists was created with minutes of zero or more.
reasoning.pitfall: Saying the check makes `minutes` unchangeable fails because that comes from `readonly`, while the check only guards the starting value.
reasoning.verify: `new Duration(-1)` throws InvalidArgumentException and `new Duration(0)` succeeds. Trying `$d->minutes = 5` afterward throws an Error, which is the separate readonly guarantee.

reasoning.approach: Add `public function label(): string` that returns the minutes with a unit, reading `$this->minutes` without assigning to it.
reasoning.pitfall: Storing the label in a second property fails because a future change to minutes could leave the label out of date.
reasoning.verify: Calling `label()` twice returns 45 minutes both times, and minutes is still 45.

reasoning.approach: Promote `string $topic` and `int $minutes` as readonly, trim and reject an empty topic, and reject negative minutes in the constructor.
